__notes__.note.transport.setting-completion-confor:
This section is standard \cite{Hestenes2001, HLR2001, DFM2007, DoranLasenby2003}; we fix conventions and, for later use, the topology. Adjoin to $\mathbb{V}$ two orthogonal directions $e_+, e_-$ with $e_+^2 = 1$, $e_-^2 = -1$, both orthogonal to $\mathbb{V}$, giving $\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$. Define the null pair
\[
\nO = \tfrac12(e_- - e_+), \qquad \nInf = e_- + e_+,
\]
so that $\nO^2 = \nInf^2 = 0$ and $\nO \cdot \nInf = -1$; the plane $H = \mathrm{span}\{\nO, \nInf\}$ they span is hyperbolic (the section “Null vectors, zero divisors, and hyperbolic planes”). Represent each point $x \in \mathbb{V}$ by
\begin{equation}
X(x) \;=\; \nO + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\, \nInf .
\end{equation}
Direct computation gives the two standard identities
\begin{equation}
X(x)^2 = 0, \qquad X(x)\cdot X(y) = -\tfrac12\, Q(x-y),
\end{equation}
so every point is represented by a null vector, and the representation is metrically faithful. Representatives are regarded projectively: a \emph{point} of the model is a null ray $[\,X\,] = \{\lambda X : \lambda \in \R^\times\}$ on the quadric
\[
\mathcal{Q} \;=\; \{[N] : N \in \mathbb{V} \oplus H,\ N \neq 0,\ N^2 = 0\}
\]
of the ambient space. Writing a general vector as $N = s\,\nO + x + t\,\nInf$ ($s, t \in \R$, $x \in \mathbb{V}$), one has $N \cdot \nInf = -s$; the rays with $s = 0$, an invariant condition since it reads $N \cdot \nInf = 0$, are not of the form $[X(x)]$ for any $x$, and we call them \emph{ideal points}. As is well known, the versor group of $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ acting by the relation displayed with \claimref{transport.noinverse} realises on $\mathcal{Q}$ the full conformal group of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$, the group of its angle-preserving transformations, with inversions realised by reflections \cite{HLR2001, Angles2008}.

\textbf{Topology.} Since the section “Totality of the transported reciprocal” makes claims about limits and continuity, we fix the topology once. Give $\mathbb{V} \oplus H \cong \R^{n+2}$ its standard topology, the projective space $P(\mathbb{V} \oplus H) = (\mathbb{V} \oplus H \setminus \{0\})/\R^{\times}$ the quotient topology, and $\mathcal{Q} \subset P(\mathbb{V} \oplus H)$ the subspace topology. Real projective space is compact and Hausdorff; the condition $N^2 = 0$ is well defined on rays (it scales by $\lambda^2$) and cuts out a closed subset; hence $\mathcal{Q}$ is compact and Hausdorff. The quotient map $\pi : N \mapsto [N]$ is continuous on nonzero vectors, and the lift $x \mapsto X(x)$ is polynomial, so $x \mapsto [X(x)]$ is continuous $\mathbb{V} \to \mathcal{Q}$. (The read-out map of Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}, which runs in the opposite direction, is written $\dsc$ and should not be confused with $\pi$.)

Note the division of labour between the two transports of the ascent. The inclusion $\Cl(p,q) \subseteq \Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ transports \emph{elements}, and fixes nothing: a null $v$ remains null and, by Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, remains without equivariant repair in the enlarged algebra. The map $X$ transports \emph{points}: it is quadratic, preserves no products, and is not an algebra map; and it is on points that the repair succeeds.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-machine-verificat:
Every computational identity in this paper has been checked by computer in exact rational arithmetic. The consolidated script \texttt{verify\_T01.py} \cite{ButlerVerifyT01}, deposited alongside the series' shared exact-arithmetic library \texttt{GA.py}, runs one hundred and fifteen checks and reports each; no floating point is used anywhere except the Moore--Penrose comparisons of the section “The hyperbolic atom as a matrix algebra: the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse”, which are float and compared at machine precision, and the script exits nonzero on any failure.

The twenty-two checks inherited from the published deposit's script cover: the hyperbolic-pair and versor identities; Lemma \claimref{transport.splitting-along-hyperbolic-plane}, including over an extension carrying a degenerate direction, where the dimension count is the essential step; all three steps of the proof of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} in $\Cl(2,1)$ and in $\Cl(3,2)$, the latter exercising the shear for \emph{every} $u$ in a three-dimensional $U$; the scale-robustness of Remark \claimref{note.transport.locality-robustness-obstruction}, the nilpotency data of Remark \claimref{note.transport.obstruction-parabolic}, and the partner parametrisation \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom} with the simple transitivity on it; both branches of Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} and the limit paths of Lemma \claimref{transport.density} over bases of signature $(1,1)$ and $(2,1)$; Proposition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form} with the fixed loci of Remark \claimref{note.transport.where-each-stratum-comes}, and Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}; and the two consistency checks of the section “Consistency checks against known theory”.

The eight checks of the section “One-dimensional extensions: where the obstruction lies, and the commuting square” cover: Theorem \claimref{transport.where-obstruction-lies-commuting-square}(a) on every even-dimensional $(p,q)$ with $2 \leq n \leq 6$, with Corollary \claimref{transport.which-residues-obstruct-which-way}'s two residue sets read off the grid, Corollary \claimref{transport.odd-lorentzian-dimension-exactly-one-real} in dimensions $3, 5, 7, 9, 11$, and Remark \claimref{note.transport.three-dimensions}'s three cases; Lemma \claimref{transport.even-subalgebra-one-dimensional-extension} on $(1,3)$ and $(2,0)$ with both signs of $\nu^2$; and Theorem \claimref{transport.where-obstruction-lies-commuting-square}(c), (d) on the whole grid, the repairs built from the signature tuple of the extension found to obstruct, with Proposition \claimref{transport.fusion-occurs-most-once} along the square (the centre of $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ computed blade-wise and found trivial, so fusion occurs at most once).

The other eighty-five checks (the taxonomy, the type-N sharpenings, type C, type P, and the clock) cover: Lemmas \claimref{transport.centre} and \claimref{transport.sign} exhaustively over \emph{all} signatures with $n \leq 8$, blade-wise, following the proofs, with the type-C criterion where it applies; the taxonomy's examples and Lemma \claimref{transport.regularity-localises-zero-divisors-idempotents}; the full Rule-2 package for the three bases $\Cl(1,0)$, $\Cl(0,3)$, $\Cl(2,1)$ and \emph{both} ascents of each, the $\gamma$-independence of every check being the computational form of Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}(3); the full Rule-1 package of Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial} and Proposition \claimref{transport.pinching-kernel} over $\Cl(1,1)$ and, for its physical relevance, $\Cl(1,3) \to \Cl(2,4)$ in dimension $64$; the type-P orbit facts with both clauses of Remark \claimref{note.transport.moore-penrose-boundary-idempotent-side}; Theorem \claimref{transport.cohomological-form-no-go} instantiated in $\Cl(2,2)$, with the torsor translation of Proposition \claimref{transport.pseudo-inverse-torsor} tested modulo the left ideal $v\,\Cl(\mathbb{V}')$ by exact membership; and Lemma \claimref{transport.conformal-gram-matrix} over five signatures, confirmed by exact congruence diagonalisation against the model lift, with Example \claimref{note.transport.exotic-embedding-inertness} realised concretely over the Gaussian rationals.

A second layer of machine checking, of a different kind, is deposited alongside: \texttt{T01\_kernel.lean} \cite{ButlerKernelT01}, seventy-six theorems in Lean 4 checked against Mathlib, with no \texttt{sorry} and no axioms beyond Lean's own. The two layers prove different things and neither replaces the other. The script checks named identities in named signatures, exactly and exhaustively within the range it enumerates; the Lean file proves the quantified statements, for every associative ring, every element, every transport history, and every $(p,q)$. Where both apply, the second subsumes the first: Lemma \claimref{transport.sign}'s two expressions for $\omega^2$ are checked blade-wise for $n \leq 8$ by the script and proved for all $p,q$ in Lean, the bridge between them being the polynomial identity $n(n-1) + 2q = (p-q)(p-q-1) + 4pq$; and Proposition \claimref{transport.fusion-occurs-most-once} is confirmed on the square by the script and proved for transport histories of every length in Lean. The Lean file is not a formalisation of this paper: it contains no Clifford algebras, no quadratic forms and no signatures, and it takes as hypotheses what this paper takes from the literature, namely semisimplicity, the injectivity of a unital homomorphism out of a simple ring, and Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}. Its header carries a concordance from each statement label used here to the theorems that carry it, and a list of what it does not cover.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-coordinate-normal: The normalisation just described is worth defining as a map in its own right, since it is the map by which answers return to the original space.
__notes__.note.transport.ascend-invert-descend: In plain terms, the classical reciprocal is a composite of three steps. To divide by $x$, first \emph{ascend}: represent the point $x$ in the completion as the null ray $[X(x)]$. Next \emph{invert}: apply the reflection $\iota$, which is total and never fails. Finally \emph{descend}: return the answer to $\mathbb{V}$ with the read-out $\dsc$. Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}(2) states that whenever $Q(x) \neq 0$ this composite gives exactly the classical answer $x/Q(x)$. When $Q(x) = 0$ the first two steps still succeed, and the composite fails only at the last: the answer $\iota[X(x)]$ exists, but it is an ideal point, and ideal points correspond to no point of the original space to which $\dsc$ could return them. The division in the completion succeeds; what fails is the return of its result to $\mathbb{V}$. The classical impossibility of dividing by a null vector is thereby relocated rather than removed: it is not a failure of the operation but a failure of the descent, and the transport explains the obstruction rather than removing it. The answer exists, and it lies permanently outside the original space.
__notes__.note.transport.classical: This is the linearise-then-normalise pattern of classical mathematics: M\"obius transformations $z \mapsto (az+b)/(cz+d)$ rendered total as linear maps on homogeneous pairs $(z,1)$ with the unnormalisable pairs $(\cdot\,,0)$ serving as the point at infinity; the homogeneous coordinates of projective geometry; the deferred ``perspective divide'' of computer graphics. All nonlinearity and all division are deferred to a single optional read-out, whose refusal is information (the answer is ideal), not failure. What Theorems \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, \claimref{transport.totality} and \claimref{transport.minimality} add to the classical picture is a mandate: for the geometric reciprocal of a quadratic space, this pattern is not one available representation among many but the \emph{unique minimal} totalisation, realised on the null cone exactly two dimensions up, with the element-level alternative provably closed.
__notes__.note.transport.two-sided-reading: Proposition \claimref{transport.pinching-kernel} and Theorem \claimref{transport.door-one-way} split the loose statement that descent is lossy into its two true halves. On transported elements the round trip is not lossy at all: it is the identity in the natural corner identification (the grade involution in Peirce coordinates; either way invertible), and the base algebra passes through the door unchanged in both directions. What cannot descend is the completion's \emph{new} content, the ladder pair and everything it generates off the diagonal, and this impossibility is a theorem about unital homomorphisms, not an artefact of choosing a particular descent map. The statement the computations support is sharper than the original: \emph{descent is invertible on the transported elements and impossible on the elements the ascent adjoined}. Compare the point-level statement of Lemma \claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}: there the descent is exact on the whole invertible locus and fails only on the ideal points, which are precisely the values the ascent added. Element-level and point-level descent lose different things, and each loses exactly what its ascent supplied.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-minimality-agains: Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified} quantifies over Clifford algebras of extensions of the quadratic space, the same normalisation used for Rule 1 in the section “Minimality among null-lift completions”. For Rule 1 the stronger, representation-independent statement was Theorem \claimref{transport.representation-independent-minimality-completion}, settled on the ambient quadric. For Rule 2 the corresponding question is settled by module theory instead, and the answer is stronger still: the fused algebra is minimal among \emph{all} simple real algebras, Clifford or not, into which the split algebra embeds unitally.
__notes__.note.transport.cost-transport-independen: Theorems \claimref{transport.representation-independent-minimality-completion} and \claimref{transport.embedding-independent-minimality-fusion} together make the picture uniform across the two rules, and in both cases stronger than the quadratic-space normalisations under which the rules were first proved minimal. For type N, what an ambient algebra must supply is a quadric large enough to host the \emph{points}, and the conformal Gram matrix quantifies it exactly. For type C, what it must supply is a \emph{module} large enough to carry both ideals faithfully with the commutant the fusion requires, and the module count quantifies that exactly, against arbitrary simple real algebras rather than Clifford targets alone. In both cases the cost is independent of the embedding, and in both cases the minimal environment is the one the transport rule constructs.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-state-machine-bec: The bookkeeping of the two rules assembles into the state machine of a figure of the original, whose one theorem is the following.
__notes__.note.transport.second-refuted-conjecture: The natural conjecture is that the two minimal completions are ``in general non-isomorphic,'' reading the distinct clock positions $d \pm 1$ as distinct algebras. The computation refutes this: the matrix-unit construction of Lemma \claimref{transport.matrix-units-peirce-isomorphism} is independent of $\gamma$, and the two ascents are isomorphic always. The conjecture and its refutation are both recorded, in the practice of this paper's the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go”, where the founding conjecture of the programme is refuted in the same way: the surviving true statement (geometric twoness, algebraic oneness) is sharper than either the conjecture or its naive negation.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-refuted-conjectur:
(The phrase \emph{minimal ascent} anticipates Theorem \claimref{transport.minimality}, which is logically independent of this section and proves the completion $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ minimal and unique; the conjecture is quoted in the form in which it was originally posed.)

The conjecture is false, not merely in the minimal ascent but in every ascent however large, as soon as $\dim \mathbb{V} \geq 3$. The refutation is the first main result of this paper.

The refutation redirects rather than terminates: what cannot be repaired is the element; what can be, as the remainder of this paper shows, is the \emph{space of points} in which the element's division is asked. The revised statement, no longer a conjecture, is proved as Theorems \claimref{transport.totality} and \claimref{transport.minimality} below: division by zero promotes not the element but the space the element belongs to, and does so uniquely, minimally, and totally.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-minimality-among-: The conformal model uses \emph{two} extra dimensions of opposite square. The following shows this is not a design choice. We first fix the class of completions over which minimality is claimed.

Two hypotheses in this definition carry weight, and both are deliberate.

The shape $X(x) = f(x) + x$ is the normalisation that makes the minimality question well posed. Without some such condition ``minimal completion'' is not yet a definite notion: any quadratic space whatever admits \emph{some} map into \emph{some} larger space, and one can always use a dimension of the ambient space to re-encode the base rather than extend it. Requiring the $\mathbb{V}$-coordinates of a represented point to be the point itself says exactly that the representation leaves the base alone and puts new structure only into the adjoined directions; the question then asked, and answered, is how much new structure that is. (Allowing an arbitrary re-embedding of $\mathbb{V}$ alongside would merely relabel the base without changing which spaces $\mathbb{W}$ can host nullity, so nothing is lost by the normalisation, and the counting becomes meaningful.) The conformal lift $X(x) \;=\; 
O + x + 	frac12 Q(x)\, 
Inf$ is a null-lift completion with $\mathbb{W} = H$ and $f(x) = 
O + 	frac12 Q(x)
Inf$, $f(0) = 
O 
eq 0$.

Nondegeneracy of $\mathbb{W}$ is the second, and Remark \claimref{note.transport.degenerate-adjunctions-why-they-are-excluded} records precisely where it is needed and what happens without it.
__notes__.note.transport.signargument: Two small arguments carry the theorem, and they deserve emphasis for how little they assume. The sign argument: the adjoined directions must be capable of cancelling squared lengths of every sign, and only a mixed addition can: new null structure appears only where positive meets negative. The origin argument: merely representing the origin as a ray already requires a null vector of $\mathbb{W}$, which forces indefiniteness even over a Euclidean base. The obstruction thereby determines its own repair, including where the repair lies. Note also the consonance with Remark \claimref{note.transport.hyperbolic-atom}: the completion adjoins precisely the hyperbolic plane, the one quadratic space that is self-complete at the level of elements, the unit of transport.
__notes__.note.transport.what-not-unique:
Uniqueness in Theorem \claimref{transport.minimality} is uniqueness of the adjoined \emph{space} $\mathbb{W}$ (up to isometry), hence of the completed algebra up to isomorphism. The lift $f$ itself is not unique: for any $c 
eq 0$, $f_c(x) = c\,
O + 	frac{1}{2c} Q(x)\,
Inf$ satisfies the same nullity condition. What is forced is the space in which the lift must lie, not how it is parametrised.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-euclidean-plane-i:
Take the base $\mathbb{V} = \R^2$ with $Q$ positive definite (signature $(2,0)$), and identify $\mathbb{V}$ with $\C = \mathrm{span}\{1, I_{2}\}$, $I_{2} = e_{1}e_{2}$ the unit bivector of the plane ($I_{2}^{2} = -1$), by $z = e_{1}(xe_{1} + ye_{2}) = x + I_{2}y$, so that $Q(z) = |z|^2$. Definite signature has no null vectors, so the partial locus of $\rho(z) = z/Q(z)$ is the origin alone: this is the oldest division by zero there is. Note which hypotheses are at work. The no-go theorem requires $p, q \geq 1$ and $n \geq 3$ and does not apply here, since with no null vectors there is no element-level question to obstruct, while the theorems this example exercises (totality, minimality, the normal form) hold in every nondegenerate signature, as recorded in the scope paragraph of the section “Quadratic spaces and Clifford algebras”.

The completion is $\Cl(3,1)$. Because $Q$ is definite, the incidence condition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form} with $s = 0$ forces $z = 0$: the ideal strata (i) and (ii) of Proposition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form} are empty, and the only ideal point is $[\nInf]$, stratum (iii). The quadric $\mathcal{Q}$ is therefore the plane with a single point adjoined, and the map
\[
[X(z)] \;\mapsto\; \frac{1}{|z|^2+1}\bigl(\,2x,\; 2y,\; |z|^2 - 1\,\bigr), \qquad [\nInf] \;\mapsto\; (0,0,1)
\]
identifies $\mathcal{Q}$ with the unit sphere $S^2 \subset \R^3$ by inverse stereographic projection from the north pole. This is the Riemann sphere, with $[X(0)]$ the south pole and $[\nInf]$ the point at infinity.

Under this identification, Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} computes
\[
\iota[X(z)] = [X(z/|z|^2)] \ \ (z \neq 0), \qquad \iota[X(0)] = [\nInf], \qquad \iota[\nInf] = [X(0)],
\]
and $z \mapsto z/|z|^2 = 1/\bar{z}$ is inversion in the unit circle. On the sphere it is the reflection
\[
(X, Y, Z) \;\mapsto\; (X, Y, -Z)
\]
in the equatorial plane: the modulus inverts and the argument is unchanged, so the equator $|z| = 1$ is fixed pointwise and the two poles, $0$ and $\infty$, are exchanged. Both statements are Proposition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form} read in these coordinates, the second being the fixed locus $\{Q = 1\} \cup \text{(ii)}$ of Remark \claimref{note.transport.where-each-stratum-comes} with the stratum (ii) that definite signature leaves empty. Inversion in a circle is anti-holomorphic; the holomorphic $z \mapsto 1/z$ of complex analysis is its composite with the reflection $y \mapsto -y$, which is a reflection of the base and so a versor of the model. Either way the content tested is the same, and it is the classical one: a reciprocal undefined at a single point of the plane becomes a total involution of a compact surface two dimensions up, with $1/0 = \infty$ and $1/\infty = 0$. Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} reproduces the nineteenth-century resolution of $1/0$ by conformal compactification, as it must, and Theorem \claimref{transport.minimality} adds that the two dimensions it uses are the fewest that will serve.

The same computation over the one-dimensional base $\mathbb{V} = \R$, $Q(x) = x^2$, has completion $\Cl(2,1)$, identifies $\mathcal{Q}$ with the real projective line $\R P^1$ in its classical homogeneous coordinates $[\,x : s\,]$, and returns for $\iota$ the classical inversion matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{psmallmatrix}$, with $[\,0:1\,]$ and $[\,1:0\,]$ exchanged.

What no definite signature exhibits, in either dimension, is the null cone. The genuinely new content of Theorems \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} and \claimref{transport.totality}(3) lies on the ideal strata (i) and (ii), which are empty here and carry, in mixed signature, one class per null vector and one per null direction respectively. There the compactification adjoins a stratum rather than a point, and the element-level question is both posed and closed.
__notes__.note.transport.bit-algebra-forgets: Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified} sharpens the disanalogy with Rule 1 into its correct form. In Rule 1 the signature increment $(+1,+1)$ is unique outright (Theorem \claimref{transport.minimality}). In Rule 2 the \emph{algebraic} completion is likewise unique (there is one fused algebra, $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$), but its geometric realisations are two, and no fusion-internal criterion distinguishes them: the sign $\gamma$ is a genuine geometric datum with no algebraic counterpart. The clock positions differ ($d + 1$ and $d - 1$ mod 8, i.e.\ residues $2$ and $0$, or $6$ and $4$), yet the classification table of Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras} is symmetric about the split residues (positions $0$ and $2$ are both real type, $4$ and $6$ both quaternionic), which is the table-level reflection of the isomorphism proved intrinsically in Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}(3). A canonical choice of $\gamma$, if one is ever wanted, must therefore be imported from structure outside the algebra (an orientation of the ambient geometry), and we record the fact here at the level of algebra only: \emph{the fusion is forced, the sign is free}.
__notes__.note.transport.three-smallest-fusions: $\Cl(1,0) \cong \R \oplus \R$: both ascents give $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(1,0)) = \Mat_2(\R)$, and indeed $\Cl(2,0) \cong \Cl(1,1) \cong \Mat_2(\R)$, the familiar coincidence that the Euclidean and Minkowski plane algebras agree, here encountered as forced by fusion uniqueness rather than as an accident of the classification table. $\Cl(0,3) \cong \HH \oplus \HH$: both ascents give $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(0,3)) = \Mat_2(\HH)$, i.e.\ $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Cl(0,4) \cong \Mat_2(\HH)$: the spacetime algebra is one of the two geometric realisations of the unique fusion of the double quaternions. $\Cl(2,1) \cong \Mat_2(\R) \oplus \Mat_2(\R)$ (the algebra of $2{+}1$-dimensional spacetime): both ascents give $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(2,1)) \cong \Mat_4(\R)$, i.e.\ $\Cl(3,1) \cong \Cl(2,2) \cong \Mat_4(\R)$.
__notes__.note.transport.what-procedure-does-not-d:
Three boundaries, each a theorem rather than a caution.

It never returns an inverse. For type N no element-level repair exists at all (Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}); what the ascent supplies is a total operation on points together with a canonical destination for the values the base cannot hold. A reader who wants $1/v$ will not find it here, and Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} is the statement that nobody will.

It assumes the form is nondegenerate. Everything above is stated for nondegenerate $(\mathbb{V},Q)$. A degenerate form is not a harder case of the same problem but a different one: its radical generates a square-zero ideal rather than a resolvable obstruction (Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified}(2) is the fibre-level instance), and completing it is the subject of the series' sheaf-theoretic paper \cite{ButlerT4}.

It is a procedure for one algebra. When division fails not at a point of an algebra but along a locus of a family, the rank of the relevant bundle cannot jump, and the correct object is a pair of sheaves rather than a single ascent: the fibrewise version of Step 3, with the completion performed over the degenerate locus and only there, is \cite[Thm.\ 4.4, Cor.\ 4.5]{ButlerT4}.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-position-series:
This paper is T1 of the series.

\emph{This paper relies on:} the companion primer T0 \cite{ButlerT0}, and on nothing else in the series. The division of labour is strict: the language belongs to the primer (the structural lemmas of the section “Setting, and the classical facts the proofs use” are restated with their toolkit numbers, and proved in the primer's toolkit \cite[Section 9]{ButlerT0}, save the classification theorem, cited there to its classical sources), while every fact about the failure of division, zero divisors, pseudo-inverses and idempotents included, is stated and proved in this paper. Beyond the toolkit the primer is a convenience for readers new to geometric algebra. The paper's other input is the founding idea of the programme itself, whose informal taxonomy it rigorises.

\emph{Papers that rely on this one:} every other research paper of the series. In brief: T2 \cite{ButlerT2} takes the element-level lemma that a square-zero element is invertible in no unital extension (Lemma \claimref{transport.noinverse}), the type-N reading of a radical direction with the taxonomy frame, and the scope of the sharpenings of the section “Minimality against arbitrary embeddings”, and proves its own completion theorem for degenerate algebras against that frame; T3 \cite{ButlerT3} iterates Rule 1 into the tower, using the Morita theorem and the pinching; T4 \cite{ButlerT4} localises the taxonomy and Rule 1 over degenerate loci, using the splitting lemma and the null-generator clause of Theorem \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified}; T5 \cite{ButlerT5} runs the whole algorithm on the black-hole singularity, importing the no-go, totality, minimality, the type-C exclusion for $\Cl(1,3)$, the pinching, and the one-way door; and the papers after T5 \cite{ButlerT5} import these results through T3 \cite{ButlerT3}, T4 \cite{ButlerT4} and T5 \cite{ButlerT5} rather than directly, with each paper's Fact environments carrying the exact provenance. The capstone T17 \cite{ButlerT17} maps the series and records the status of every claim.

One subsection points forward without relying on anything: the sentence after Corollary \claimref{transport.which-residues-obstruct-which-way} names the dark-matter paper T14 \cite{ButlerT14} for the residues $\{2, 6\}$. It is a pointer, and the theorems of the section “One-dimensional extensions: where the obstruction lies, and the commuting square” use only this paper.
__notes__.note.transport.exotic-embedding-inertnes: $\Cl(1,3) \cong \Mat_2(\HH)$ embeds unitally in $\Cl(2,3) \cong \Mat_4(\C)$, an algebra of \emph{half} the dimension of the completion $\Cl(2,4)$: the standard unital embedding $\HH \hookrightarrow \Mat_2(\C)$ ($1, i, j, k$, Hamilton's units, mapped to $I$, $\mathrm{diag}(I_5, -I_5)$, $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$, $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&I_5\\I_5&0\end{psmallmatrix}$, the matrix entries read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_5\}$, the centre of $\Cl(2,3)$, whose pseudoscalar $I_5$ is its complex unit, Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}) applied entrywise gives $\Mat_2(\HH) \hookrightarrow \Mat_4(\C)$, and $\Cl(2,3)$ has type $\Mat_4(\C)$ by Theorem \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras} ($d \equiv 7$). The embedding is genuine; it is also inert: the ambient quadratic space of $\Cl(2,3)$ is five-dimensional, and by Theorem \claimref{transport.representation-independent-minimality-completion} no normalised conformal chart of four-dimensional spacetime exists on its quadric. The algebra is big enough to contain $\Cl(1,3)$ and too small to resolve it: what a resolution needs is not space for the \emph{elements} but space for the \emph{points}, and points cost two dimensions in the exact balance $(+1,+1)$.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-mod-8-clock-one-w: The two rules now proved, this section settles their bookkeeping: how transport moves the algebra's Morita class (it almost never does), and what survives descent (everything transported; nothing adjoined). Both answers turn on the same construction used for Rule 2: matrix units, this time supplied by the ascent itself.
__notes__.note.transport.prior-art-what-new-here: The isomorphism $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl(p,q))$ is classical: it is the algebraic form of the $(1,1)$-periodicity of Clifford algebras \cite{ABS1964, Porteous1995, Lounesto2001}, usually obtained from $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1) \cong \Cl(p,q)\,\hat{\otimes}\,\Cl(1,1)$ and $\Cl(1,1) \cong \Mat_2(\R)$. What we claim as expository contribution is the presentation: the matrix units \emph{are} the transported ladder pair and its occupation projectors, so the periodicity isomorphism is not auxiliary to the transport principle but is the transport principle's own bookkeeping: the ascent adjoins exactly one row and column's worth of new structure, and the relations $f^2 = 0$, $ff^* + f^*f = 1$ are the matrix-unit relations of that adjunction. The parallel with Rule 2 is now exact (Remark \claimref{note.transport.2-pattern-two-rules-compared}): both rules amplify by $\Mat_2$, Rule 1 over the whole base, Rule 2 over its even half, and in both cases the matrix units are built from the completion's own canonical elements: the ladder pair for N, the central projectors plus the adjoined generator for C.
__notes__.note.transport.iteration: Iterating Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial} gives $\Cl(p{+}k, q{+}k) \cong \Mat_{2^k}(\Cl(p,q))$: the tower over any base is Morita-stationary from its first step. The structural consequences of the iterated statement (tower rigidity, the one-mode-per-rung reading, and the direct limit) are the subject of the series' tower paper \cite{ButlerT3} and are not developed here.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-one-way-door-what: The asymmetry of transport (total on the way up, lossy on the way down) is now made exact in the matrix picture of Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}. Throughout, $P = f^*f$ and $1 - P = ff^*$ are the \emph{descent projectors}, the diagonal matrix units; they are the spectral projections $\tfrac12(1 \pm \sigma)$ of the involution $\sigma = f^*f - ff^*$, $\sigma^2 = 1$, canonically attached to the completed pair.
__notes__.note.transport.2-pattern-two-rules-compa: Both minimal ascents turn out to be $2 \times 2$ matrix amplifications, of the whole algebra for type N and of its even half for type C (the section “The mod-8 clock and the one-way door” proves the first and reads both as the transport's own bookkeeping). The comparison exposes the cost asymmetry precisely: Rule 1 adds two dimensions and preserves the Morita class, $d$ fixed; Rule 2 adds one dimension, halves the coefficient algebra to its even part, and moves $d$ by $\pm 1$.
__notes__.note.transport.destination:
The geometric content of (3), for a null vector $v$: the value of ``division by $v$'' is an ideal point at null infinity \emph{determined by} $v$: it lies over the null direction of $v$, at a position fixed by the scale of $v$. The value remembers more than the direction alone: rescaling $v$ moves it, $[\,2v + 	frac12
Inf\,] 
eq [\,v + 	frac12
Inf\,]$ (in the coordinates of Proposition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form}, these are distinct points of the same ideal stratum). The answer to the forbidden division exists and is canonical; it merely does not lie in the original space. Together with Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, this is the precise sense in which the ascent performs ``division by zero without an inverse operation'': the element remains non-invertible; the space of points acquires a value for the division.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-coordinate-normal: The mechanism of Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} admits a coordinate statement that identifies it with a classical pattern. (The scalar slots are written $s, t$ to avoid collision with the $\Cl(U')$-coefficients $\alpha, \beta$ of the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go”.)
__notes__.note.transport.where-each-stratum-comes: The three strata are distinguished by $\iota$ itself, which supplies a check on the bookkeeping. Stratum (i) is exactly the image of the null cone of $\mathbb{V}$ under $\iota \circ X$, and (iii) is the image of the origin. Stratum (ii) is the image of neither: it is fixed \emph{pointwise} by $\iota$, since $(0,x,0) \mapsto (0,x,0)$. Indeed the whole fixed locus of $\iota$ is $\{Q(x) = 1\} \cup \text{(ii)}$, as one sees by solving $(2t, x, \tfrac12 s) = \lambda(s,x,t)$ against \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form}: $\lambda = 1$ forces $s = 2t$ and $Q(x) = 4t^2$, which after normalisation is the unit quadric when $t \neq 0$ and stratum (ii) when $t = 0$. So the null directions at infinity are the ideal fixed points of the inversion, as they must be: they are the directions along which the null cone through the origin goes to infinity, and inversion carries that cone to itself.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-null-vectors-zero:
Null vectors are moreover two-sided zero divisors. The obstruction they pose is packaged in the reciprocal map
\[
\rho : \mathbb{V} \setminus \{Q = 0\} \to \mathbb{V}, \qquad \rho(x) = x / Q(x),
\]
which is partial exactly on $\{Q = 0\}$, the null cone together with the origin. Both failure modes are resolved by the same completion (Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}); only the null cone poses the element-level question of the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go”, the pseudo-inverse condition being vacuous at the origin.

Null vectors come in pairs. If $v$ is null and $Q$ is nondegenerate, there is a vector $a$ with $v \cdot a \neq 0$; rescaling so that $v \cdot a = \tfrac12$ and setting $w = a - Q(a)\,v$ gives
\[
Q(w) = Q(a) - 2\,Q(a)\,(v \cdot a) = 0, \qquad v \cdot w = v \cdot a = \tfrac12 :
\]
a \emph{hyperbolic pair} $(v, w)$. The plane $H = \mathrm{span}\{v, w\}$ is a \emph{hyperbolic plane}: its Gram matrix on $(v,w)$ has determinant $-\tfrac14$, so $H$ is nondegenerate of signature $(1,1)$, and conversely every two-dimensional nondegenerate space containing a null vector is isometric to $H$ \cite{Lam2005}. Inside the Clifford algebra a hyperbolic pair satisfies
\begin{equation}
v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v .
\end{equation}
The last identity says $w$ is a \emph{pseudo-inverse} of $v$ in the sense of von Neumann: division by $v$ cannot be undone exactly, but $w$ undoes it up to the defect of $v$. This is the weakened form of inversion around which the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go” revolves.
__notes__.note.transport.hyperbolic-atom:
The assumption $n \geq 3$ is necessary, and the bound is sharp. For $n = 2$ the space is itself a hyperbolic plane, $U = 0$, there are no null rotations, and the assignment $\sigma(\lambda v) = \lambda^{-1} w_0$, $\sigma(\lambda w_0) = \lambda^{-1} v$ defines a genuinely $\Pin(1,1)$-equivariant pseudo-inverse section in the sense of Definition \claimref{obj.transport.equivariance}, and no ascent is needed: the hyperbolic plane is self-complete \emph{at the level of elements}. (Its reciprocal on \emph{points} is of course still partial; Theorem \claimref{transport.totality} applies to it like any other base, and its own transport is $\Cl(2,2)$. The two senses of completion are exactly the two halves of the transport principle, and the atom separates them.)

The section has a coordinate-free description, which is the real reason for its equivariance and simultaneously explains the failure for $n \geq 3$. For null $x$, call $y$ a \emph{partner} of $x$ if $y$ is null with $x \cdot y = \tfrac12$. Writing $y = av + bw_0 + u$ with $u \in U$, the two conditions read $b = 1$ and $a = -Q(u)$, so the partners of $v$ are exactly
\begin{equation}
y_u \;=\; w_0 - u - Q(u)\,v \qquad (u \in U),
\end{equation}
an affine space of dimension $n - 2$ on which, by Step 2 of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, the null rotations act simply transitively. For $n = 2$ it is a single point, so ``the partner of $x$'' is a well-formed metric description and $\sigma$ is equivariant for that reason alone, with no computation; for $n \geq 3$ a torsor has no distinguished point, and Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} says no enlargement of the space produces one. This is precisely why the hyperbolic plane is the unit of transport: the ascent of the section “The completion: the conformal model” adjoins a copy of the one quadratic space that needs no ascent of the first kind.


The same dimension count is Zeeman's. By Zeeman's theorem \cite{Zeeman1964}, for $n \geq 3$ every bijection of Minkowski space preserving the causal order is generated by Lorentz transformations, translations and dilations, while in $n = 2$ the two null coordinates can be reparametrised independently and the causal automorphism group is infinite-dimensional. The two-dimensional counterexamples to Zeeman are exactly the freedom that the null rotations remove for $n \geq 3$ by mixing each null direction with the transverse ones; the little group of a null direction has a null-rotation part of dimension $n - 2$, and both theorems hold precisely when it is present. Zeeman's theorem is imported here, not proved, and nothing below depends on it; this paragraph records that the third hypothesis of Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements} and Zeeman's are the same hypothesis, the existence of a null rotation, so that the hyperbolic atom is the exception to both for one reason.

__notes__.note.transport.setting-destination-advan:
Section \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm} turns the theorems into a six-step procedure. It asks, in order:

   
\begin{enumerate}
  
\item Where does division fail?
\item Which of the three obstructions is it?
\item What is the minimal repair, and what does it adjoin?
\item How is the value at the obstruction computed?
\item What does descent back to the original algebra cost?
\item Does repeating the repair terminate?
\end{enumerate}
 \noindent The answers take the form of an algorithm: six steps, each with a theorem licensing it. It is set out as the table accompanying \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm} in Section \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm}, which names every step's instrument and its warrant, and which T5 follows in order.

Everything between here and there builds that algorithm. Each section proves the results that one or more of the steps invoke, one obstruction type at a time, and no step is stated before the theorem that licenses it, which is why the procedure itself comes last rather than first. A reader who would rather see the destination before the route can read the table accompanying \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm} now and return here.

\emph{A reading route.} Read straight through for the mathematics in the order it was found. To enter directly: the no-go and its cohomological form are the section “The refuted conjecture, and the no-go” and the section “The obstruction as a cohomology class”; the completion, its totality and its two minimality theorems are the section “The completion: the conformal model” to the section “Minimality against arbitrary embeddings”; the fusion theorem is the section “The fusion theorem”; the clock is the section “The mod-8 clock and the one-way door”; the algorithm is Section \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm}. the section “Setting, and the classical facts the proofs use” is notation and imported classical facts, and is meant to be consulted rather than read.

__notes__.note.transport.worked-instance: The procedure is run end to end, on the case that motivated the programme, in the series' gravitational paper \cite{ButlerT5}, whose chain of steps mirrors the table accompanying \claimref{transport.transport-algorithm} row for row. It is worth carrying the outline through the paper as a running example. In it: the failure is located at the centre of the Schwarzschild solution, where the light cones fold onto a single direction (Step 1); the degenerating direction is null and the algebra $\Cl(1,3)$ is simple, with $d \equiv 6 \bmod 8$, so the diagnosis is type N and type C is unavailable (Step 2, by Theorem \claimref{transport.existence-classification-type-c} and Example \claimref{note.transport.cl-1-3-physical-case-n}); Rule 1 gives $\Cl(1,3) \to \Cl(2,4)$, the conformal algebra of spacetime, forced (Step 3); the transported division is total there (Step 4); and the descent is lossy in exactly the way Step 5 states, which is where that paper's physical content begins. The example is worth keeping in view for one reason in particular: the answer to the forbidden division is not a number in spacetime, and the algorithm says so in advance rather than after the fact.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-transport-algorit: The six steps are the whole paper in operational form: the section “Setting, and the classical facts the proofs use” and the section “A taxonomy of obstructions” supplied Steps 1 and 2; the section “Type N: the isotropic obstruction, and Rule 1” supplied Steps 3 to 5 for the hard type, which took half the paper; the section “Type C: ideal fusion, and Rule 2” and the section “Type P: the rule of no rule” supplied Step 3 for the other two types; and the section “The mod-8 clock and the one-way door” supplied Step 6.
__notes__.note.transport.setting-transport-princip:
The Principle is a summary, not an axiom: each of its clauses is one of the theorems proved above, and it adds nothing to them. What it does add is the reading. The three costs are not a graded scale of difficulty but three different answers to one equivariance question, and the question is answerable at all only because the taxonomy is exhaustive: it is the completeness of Theorem \claimref{transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent}, not the ingenuity of any rule, that turns a family of repairs into a procedure.

Two closing observations. First, the shape of the type-N answer is the surprising one, and it is worth stating plainly that it is a change of level rather than a technical fix: what is repaired is not the element, which remains non-invertible in every enlargement however large, but the space in which the element's division was asked. Second, no transport removes all obstructions. Every completion carries obstructions of its own, and in the type-N case the adjoined pair is itself null (Proposition \claimref{transport.no-transport-terminates}): the repair of the old null cone is effected by adjoining new members of it. What the bookkeeping of the section “The mod-8 clock and the one-way door” shows is therefore not that transport terminates but that it stabilises, the clock moving at most once and then remaining fixed. Obstruction is conserved; what the rules achieve is that it no longer changes the Wedderburn type.

The paper is intended to be independently checkable throughout: every algebraic statement can be verified from the axiom $v^2 = Q(v)$ with pencil and paper, the topological statements of the section “Totality of the transported reciprocal” from the elementary point-set facts recorded in the section “The completion: the conformal model”, and every computational identity by the deposited scripts.

conformal.nilpotent-ideal-becomes-unit-i.formal:
Fix a basis $\rho_1, \dots, \rho_r$ of $R$. In $\Cl(p,q,r)$ the radical generates the two-sided ideal $J = \sum_i \Cl \cdot \rho_i$, with
\[
\dim J = 2^m - 2^{m-r}, \qquad J^{\,r+1} = 0, \qquad J^{\,r} \neq 0 ;
\]
in particular $J^2 = 0$ precisely when $r = 1$, the corank-one case established at sheaf level in \cite[Thm.~3.1]{ButlerT4}. In any completion, the image of the radical generates the \emph{unit} ideal of the ambient Clifford algebra, and each radical basis vector spans a hyperbolic plane with a partner vector of the completion.
conformal.nilpotent-ideal-becomes-unit-i.technical:
Fix a basis $\rho_1,\dots,\rho_r$ of the radical $R$. In $\Cl(p,q,r)$ the radical generates the two-sided ideal $J = \sum_i \Cl\cdot\rho_i$, spanned by the blades that contain at least one radical letter, so $\dim J = 2^m - 2^{m-r}$. Radical letters have $Q(\rho_i) = 0$, anticommute with every vector and are never contracted away, so $J^{r+1} = 0$, while the nonzero blade $\rho_1\cdots\rho_r$ shows $J^r \neq 0$; in particular $J^2 = 0$ exactly when $r = 1$.

In any completion each $\rho_i$ has a partner $\varphi_i$ with $Q(\rho_i,\varphi_i) = 1$, which can be chosen null, so $\operatorname{span}\{\rho_i,\varphi_i\}$ is a hyperbolic plane. The Clifford relation $\rho_i\varphi_i + \varphi_i\rho_i = 2$ then places $1$ in the ideal generated by $\rho_i$: the image of the radical generates the unit ideal of the ambient algebra.
conformal.nilpotent-ideal-becomes-unit-i.lay: In a degenerate geometric algebra the degenerate directions generate a family of elements that multiply to zero once enough of them are combined, the number needed being one more than the number of degenerate directions. None of these elements can be inverted, and no enlargement changes that. Once the space is completed, however, each degenerate direction gains a partner, and the two together produce the number one, so the obstruction disappears at the level of the whole algebra rather than by giving any single element an inverse.
conformal.nilpotent-ideal-becomes-unit-i.typing_note: Removed the sheaf-paper resolution result, which the proof cites only as the infinite-dimensional analogue of its last step; the corank-one sheaf theorem in the statement is likewise a comparison and was not added.

proofs.main:
\emph{The mechanics of radical letters.} Work in the blade basis (Fact \claimref{conformal.blade-basis-persists-under-degeneracy}) adapted to a decomposition $W = V_1 \oplus R$: each blade is $x_T\, \rho_S$ with $x_T$ a blade in a basis of $V_1$ and $\rho_S := \rho_{s_1} \cdots \rho_{s_j}$, $S = \{s_1 < \dots < s_j\}$. A radical letter $\rho$ satisfies $B(\rho, z) = 0$ for every vector $z$, so $\rho z = -z\rho$ with no scalar term: in any product of blades, radical letters reorder by pure anticommutation and contract with nothing, while a repeated radical letter makes the product zero ($\rho^2 = 0$). Hence
\[
(x_T\, \rho_S)(x_{T'}\, \rho_{S'}) \;=\;
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } S \cap S' \neq \emptyset, \\
\pm\, (x_T\, x_{T'})\; \rho_{S \cup S'} & \text{if } S \cap S' = \emptyset ,
\end{cases}
\]
where $x_T\, x_{T'}$ expands over blades of $V_1$ alone: radical letters accumulate and are never contracted away.

The ideal, its dimension and its nilpotency index are parts (i) and (ii) of Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.radical-ideal-and-quotient} for the space of signature $(p, q, r)$; in the blade notation above they read as follows.

\emph{The ideal, and its dimension.} $\mathcal{S} := \operatorname{span}\{x_T \rho_S : S \neq \emptyset\}$ is a two-sided ideal by the display, and it equals $J$: every $x_T \rho_S$ with $s_1 \in S$ lies in $\Cl \cdot \rho_{s_1} \cdot \Cl$, and conversely every product $a \rho_i b$ expands into blades each retaining the letter $\rho_i$. Counting blades with $S \neq \emptyset$ gives $\dim J = 2^m - 2^{m-r}$.

\emph{Nilpotency, and its exact index.} By the display, a product of $j$ elements of $J$ lies in the span of blades carrying at least $j$ radical letters; only $r$ radical letters exist, so $J^{\,r+1} = 0$. In the other direction, $\rho_1 \cdots \rho_r$ is a product of $r$ elements of $J$ and is a basis blade, hence nonzero: $J^{\,r} \neq 0$. For $r \geq 2$ the nonzero blade $\rho_1 \rho_2 \in J^2$ shows the ideal is not square-zero.

\emph{The unit ideal in the completion.} Let $(\widetilde W, Q)$ be any completion and $\rho_i$ a radical basis vector. By nondegeneracy there is $\varphi_i \in \widetilde W$ with $Q(\rho_i, \varphi_i) = 1$, so the Clifford relation (\claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}) gives $\rho_i \varphi_i + \varphi_i \rho_i = 2$, and $1 = \tfrac12(\rho_i \varphi_i + \varphi_i \rho_i)$ lies in the two-sided ideal generated by $\rho_i$ (both summands carry the factor $\rho_i$). Replacing $\varphi_i$ by $\varphi_i - \tfrac12 Q(\varphi_i, \varphi_i)\, \rho_i$ leaves $Q(\rho_i, \varphi_i) = 1$ (since $Q(\rho_i, \rho_i) = 0$) and makes $\varphi_i$ null, so $\operatorname{span}\{\rho_i, \varphi_i\}$ is a hyperbolic plane. This is the finite-dimensional instance of the resolution mechanism of \cite[Prop.~3.4]{ButlerT4}.

conformal.principal-case.formal: $\mathrm{PGA} = \Cl(3,0,1)$ has minimal nondegenerate completion $\Cl(4,1) = \mathrm{CGA}$, uniquely: the engineering community's two standard algebras are a degenerate algebra and its unique minimal completion. Likewise in the plane, $\Cl(2,0,1)$ completes minimally to $\Cl(3,1)$; and in general the $n$-dimensional Euclidean PGA $\Cl(n,0,1)$ completes minimally to the $n$-dimensional CGA $\Cl(n{+}1,1)$.
conformal.principal-case.technical:
Apply the minimal completion theorem with $(p,q,r) = (n,0,1)$. The Euclidean projective algebra $\Cl(n,0,1)$, with one null generator, has a minimal nondegenerate completion of dimension $n+2$ and signature $(n+1,1)$, unique up to an isometry fixing the original space, so $\Cl(n,0,1) \hookrightarrow \Cl(n+1,1)$, the $n$-dimensional conformal algebra.

For $n = 3$ this says that $\mathrm{PGA} = \Cl(3,0,1)$ completes minimally and uniquely to $\mathrm{CGA} = \Cl(4,1)$, and for $n = 2$ that $\Cl(2,0,1)$ completes to $\Cl(3,1)$.
conformal.principal-case.lay: Engineers and graphics programmers use two geometric algebras: projective geometric algebra, which has one degenerate direction standing for the plane at infinity, and conformal geometric algebra, which has two extra directions. They are usually treated as separate design choices. This result shows that the conformal algebra is the unique smallest nondegenerate enlargement of the projective one, in any number of dimensions, in the sense of enlarging the underlying space.
conformal.principal-case.typing_note: Single premise is the minimal completion theorem specialised to one null generator; the paper presents the PGA to CGA identification as new, so no standard route.

proofs.main: Theorem \claimref{conformal.minimal-nondegenerate-completion} with $(p,q,r) = (n,0,1)$.

conformal.witt-extension-theorem.formal: Over a field of characteristic not two, let $(\widetilde W_1, Q_1)$ and $(\widetilde W_2, Q_2)$ be isometric nondegenerate quadratic spaces and let $\sigma : S_1 \to S_2$ be an isometry between subspaces $S_i \subseteq \widetilde W_i$, the $S_i$ arbitrary and possibly degenerate. Then $\sigma$ extends to an isometry $\widetilde W_1 \to \widetilde W_2$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Ch.~I, Thm.~4.7]{Lam2005}.
conformal.witt-extension-theorem.technical:
Over a field of characteristic not two, let $(\widetilde W_1,Q_1)$ and $(\widetilde W_2,Q_2)$ be isometric nondegenerate quadratic spaces and let $\sigma: S_1 \to S_2$ be an isometry between subspaces $S_i \subseteq \widetilde W_i$, which may be degenerate. Then $\sigma$ extends to an isometry $\widetilde W_1 \to \widetilde W_2$.

This is the classical Witt extension theorem of the algebraic theory of quadratic forms. In the series it is what makes minimal completions unique up to an isometry fixing the original space.
conformal.witt-extension-theorem.lay: Suppose two spaces carry equivalent nondegenerate notions of length and angle. Then any length-preserving match between a part of one and a part of the other can be extended to a length-preserving match of the whole spaces. This works even when the parts themselves are degenerate. It is a standard theorem about quadratic forms.

imported_from.citation: T. Y. Lam, Introduction to Quadratic Forms over Fields, Graduate Studies in Mathematics 67, American Mathematical Society (2005).

conformal.witt-extension-theorem.typing_note: Imported textbook result; levels describe the classical theorem only.

correspondence.imported-forced-completio.formal: Division by a type-N zero divisor in $\Cl(1,3)$ admits no element-level resolution (the transvection no-go), and the minimal completion resolving it is $\Cl(1,3) \hookrightarrow \Cl(2,4)$, unique up to isomorphism; the resolving assignments lie on the quadric of null rays of $\R^{2,4}$, the completion's point space. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thms.~4.2, 4.10, 4.13]{ButlerT1}; representation-independent minimality \cite[\S4.6]{ButlerT1}.
correspondence.imported-forced-completio.technical:
Division by a type-N zero divisor in the spacetime algebra $\Cl(1,3)$ has no element-level resolution: this is the transvection no-go. The minimal completion that resolves it is $\Cl(1,3) \hookrightarrow \Cl(2,4)$, adjoining one hyperbolic plane, and it is unique up to isomorphism.

The resolving assignments lie on the quadric of null rays of $\R^{2,4}$, which is the point space of the completion. The statement restates earlier series results on the no-go, on totality of the transported reciprocal and on minimality.
correspondence.imported-forced-completio.lay: In the algebra of spacetime some elements cannot be divided by, and nothing done inside the algebra fixes this. The smallest enlargement that does fix it adds two dimensions, one space-like and one time-like, and this enlargement is unique. The repaired divisions live on the set of light-like directions of the resulting six-dimensional space.

correspondence.imported-forced-completio.typing_note: The three uses are exactly the root-paper no-go, totality and minimality results the Fact cites; the representation-independent sharpening it also cites has no separate store entry.

obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces.formal: An \emph{extension} of the nondegenerate quadratic space $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is a real quadratic space $(\mathbb{V}', Q')$ with $\mathbb{V} \subseteq \mathbb{V}'$ and $Q'|_{\mathbb{V}} = Q$. The form $Q'$ is not assumed nondegenerate. Because $Q$ is nondegenerate on $\mathbb{V}$, the extension splits orthogonally and automatically: $\mathbb{V}' = \mathbb{V} \perp \mathbb{V}^{\perp}$, where $\mathbb{V}^{\perp} = \{ a \in \mathbb{V}' : a \cdot x = 0 \ \forall x \in \mathbb{V}\}$ \cite{Lam2005}. Extensions in this sense are exactly the ``ascents'' quantified over in Theorem \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}.
obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces.technical:
An extension of a nondegenerate quadratic space $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is a real quadratic space $(\mathbb{V}', Q')$ with $\mathbb{V} \subseteq \mathbb{V}'$ and $Q'|_{\mathbb{V}} = Q$; the form $Q'$ may be degenerate. Because $Q$ is nondegenerate on $\mathbb{V}$, every extension splits orthogonally, $\mathbb{V}' = \mathbb{V} \perp \mathbb{V}^\perp$.

These extensions are exactly the ascents over which the element-level no-go result quantifies.
obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces.lay: An extension places a space with a notion of length inside a larger space whose notion of length agrees with the original on the original vectors. The larger space is allowed to have directions of zero length. Because the original space is nondegenerate, the larger one always splits into the original plus a part perpendicular to it.
obj.transport.extension-quadratic-spaces.typing_note: Definition; levels explain it and its automatic orthogonal splitting.

history.text: About from the statements that quantify over every extension of the base quadratic space.

obj.transport.normalised-conformal-chart.formal:
Let $(\mathbb{V}'', Q'')$ be a nondegenerate real quadratic space. A \emph{normalised conformal chart} of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ in $\mathbb{V}''$ is a map $\Phi : \mathbb{V} \to \mathbb{V}''$ with
\[
\Phi(x) \cdot \Phi(y) \;=\; -\tfrac12\, Q(x - y) \qquad \text{for all } x, y \in \mathbb{V}
\]
(in particular every $\Phi(x)$ is null, and $\Phi$ is injective by nondegeneracy). This is exactly the metric-faithfulness identity $X(x)^2 = 0, \qquad X(x)\cdot X(y) = -\tfrac12\, Q(x-y)$ of the conformal model; the lift $X$ of the completion is a normalised conformal chart, and any projective chart with a nowhere-vanishing scale is rescaled into this form. Nothing else is assumed of $\Phi$: not linearity, not continuity.
obj.transport.normalised-conformal-chart.technical:
Let $(\mathbb{V}'', Q'')$ be a nondegenerate real quadratic space. A normalised conformal chart of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ in it is any map $\Phi: \mathbb{V} \to \mathbb{V}''$ with $\Phi(x)\cdot\Phi(y) = -\tfrac12 Q(x-y)$ for all $x, y$.

Taking $x = y$ shows that every $\Phi(x)$ is null, and nondegeneracy makes $\Phi$ injective. Neither linearity nor continuity is assumed. The lift of the conformal completion is such a chart, and any projective chart with a nowhere-vanishing scale can be rescaled into this form.
obj.transport.normalised-conformal-chart.lay: A normalised conformal chart places each point of a space on a light-like vector in a larger space, so that the inner product of the images of two points gives, up to a fixed factor, the squared separation of the points. Nothing else is required of the map. The usual conformal model of geometry is one such chart.
obj.transport.normalised-conformal-chart.typing_note: Definition; levels explain the metric-faithfulness identity and that no regularity is assumed.

obj.transport.null-lift-completion.formal:
A \emph{null-lift completion} of the nondegenerate quadratic space $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is a pair $(\mathbb{W}, f)$ where $\mathbb{W}$ is a nondegenerate real quadratic space adjoined orthogonally to $\mathbb{V}$ and $f : \mathbb{V} \to \mathbb{W}$ is a map with $f(0) \neq 0$ such that
\[
X(x) \;=\; f(x) + x \ \in\ \mathbb{W} \perp \mathbb{V}
\]
is null for every $x \in \mathbb{V}$. The condition $f(0) \neq 0$ says only that the origin, like every point, is represented by a nonzero vector, hence by a ray. Nothing else is assumed of $f$: not linearity, not continuity, not injectivity.
obj.transport.null-lift-completion.technical:
A null-lift completion of a nondegenerate quadratic space $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is a pair $(\mathbb{W}, f)$, where $\mathbb{W}$ is a nondegenerate real quadratic space adjoined orthogonally to $\mathbb{V}$ and $f: \mathbb{V} \to \mathbb{W}$ is a map with $f(0) \neq 0$, such that $X(x) = f(x) + x \in \mathbb{W} \perp \mathbb{V}$ is null for every $x \in \mathbb{V}$.

The condition $f(0) \neq 0$ says that the origin, like every other point, is represented by a nonzero vector and hence by a ray. Nothing else is assumed of $f$: not linearity, continuity or injectivity.
obj.transport.null-lift-completion.lay: A null-lift completion adds extra perpendicular directions to a space and attaches to each point a vector in those new directions, chosen so that the combined vector has zero length. Every point, the origin included, then becomes a light-like ray. The rule that attaches the extra vector can be any function at all.
obj.transport.null-lift-completion.typing_note: Definition; levels explain it, stressing that no regularity of the map is assumed.

obj.transport.transport.formal: The \emph{transport} of a nondegenerate $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is the pair consisting of the minimal completion $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ of Theorem \claimref{transport.minimality} and the null-ray representation $X(x) \;=\; \nO + x + \tfrac12 Q(x)\, \nInf$; the \emph{transported reciprocal} is the total involution $\iota$ of Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}. For a type-C obstruction the corresponding transport is the one-generator ascent of Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}; for type P it is the identity.
obj.transport.transport.technical:
The transport of a nondegenerate $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ of signature $(p,q)$ is the pair formed by the minimal completion $\Cl(p,q) \hookrightarrow \Cl(p+1,q+1)$ and the null-ray representation of points. The transported reciprocal is the total involution $\iota$ on null rays.

For a type-C obstruction the transport is instead the one-generator ascent of Rule 2, and for a type-P obstruction it is the identity.
obj.transport.transport.lay: Transport is the series' name for its standard way of handling a failure of division in a geometric algebra. In the basic case one adds a pair of directions and represents points as light-like rays, on which a reciprocal is defined everywhere. For one other kind of failure a single direction is added, and for a third kind nothing changes.
obj.transport.transport.typing_note: Definition; levels name the three cases without claiming more than the definition.

odd-extensions.imported-conformal-comple.formal: A shadow of signature $(t,s)$ has conformal completion with ambient of signature $(t+1, s+1)$, one rung up its own tower; for this world the ambient is $(2,4)$ and its conformal spin group acts on the conformal spinor space $\CS \cong \C^{4}$ (twistor space), whose complex unit is $I_6$, through $\Cl^{0}(2,4)$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Fact~2.1, Thm.~3.4]{ButlerT9}; \cite[Fact~2.11]{ButlerT12}.
odd-extensions.imported-conformal-comple.technical:
A shadow of signature $(t,s)$ has a conformal completion whose ambient has signature $(t+1,s+1)$, one rung up its own tower. For this world the ambient signature is $(2,4)$, and its conformal spin group acts on the conformal spinor space $\CS \cong \C^4$, with complex unit $I_6$, through the even subalgebra $\Cl^0(2,4)$.

The statement restates earlier series results on the forced completion, the spinor identification and the Fock representation of a Clifford algebra.
odd-extensions.imported-conformal-comple.lay: A space-time of any signature can be enlarged by one extra direction of each kind, its conformal completion, which is the next step up its own ladder of algebras. For our four-dimensional world this gives a six-dimensional space with two time directions, whose spin symmetries act on a four-dimensional space of spinors whose complex unit is the algebra's own pseudoscalar.

odd-extensions.imported-minimal-completi.formal: A real quadratic space with nondegenerate part of signature $(p,q)$ and radical of dimension $r$ admits a nondegenerate completion; every completion has dimension at least $p + q + 2r$; the minimal ones have signature exactly $(p+r, q+r)$; and any two minimal completions are isometric by an isometry fixing the original space pointwise, so the minimal ambient Clifford algebra $\Cl(p+r, q+r)$ is unique up to an isomorphism fixing the embedded $\Cl(p,q;r)$. In the model completion the radical is paired with its dual, $Q(\rho, \varphi) = 1$, $Q(\varphi,\varphi) = 0$, $\varphi$ orthogonal to the nondegenerate part. For a type-N obstruction in a nondegenerate algebra the increment $(+1,+1)$ is forced outright; for a type-C obstruction the completed algebra is unique but the sign of the adjoined generator's square is a geometric datum the algebra forgets. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thm.~2.3 and its model]{ButlerT2}; \cite[Thm.~4.13, Thm.~5.7 and Rem.~5.8]{ButlerT1}.
odd-extensions.imported-minimal-completi.technical:
A real quadratic space with nondegenerate part of signature $(p,q)$ and radical of dimension $r$ has nondegenerate completions, all of dimension at least $p+q+2r$. The minimal ones have signature $(p+r,q+r)$ and are unique up to an isometry fixing the original space, so $\Cl(p+r,q+r)$ is unique up to an isomorphism fixing $\Cl(p,q;r)$. In the model completion each radical vector $\rho$ is paired with a dual $\varphi$, with $Q(\rho,\varphi) = 1$, $Q(\varphi) = 0$ and $\varphi$ orthogonal to the nondegenerate part.

For a type-N obstruction in a nondegenerate algebra the increment $(+1,+1)$ is forced outright. For a type-C obstruction the completed algebra is unique, but the sign $Q(\nu) = \pm 1$ of the adjoined generator is a geometric datum the algebra forgets.
odd-extensions.imported-minimal-completi.lay: When a geometric algebra has degenerate directions, the smallest way to remove them adds one partner for each, and the result is unique. For the basic kind of division failure in an ordinary algebra, the repair must add one positive and one negative direction. For another kind, adding a single direction of either sign gives the same algebra, so the algebra alone cannot tell which sign was chosen.

odd-extensions.two-classes-completion.formal: The sheaf paper's conservation theorem concerns completions with one exterior model: the same nondegenerate complement $K$ on both sides of the wall. For those, degeneracy is conserved and displaced to a shadow wall, and the ambient adjoins a hyperbolic plane to the whole bundle: rank two by Fact \claimref{odd-extensions.imported-minimal-completion-degenerate-algebra-rule}, and to the whole bundle because off the wall the bundle is nondegenerate and the standard complement must exist there. The $\Lambda$ family is completed by a construction of the other class: a family of hyperplanes in one fixed nondegenerate space, whose complement is a single line that changes type across the wall, rank one. Nothing prevents a spacetime wall from being completed in the second class as well, with a complement that is not standard; what the sheaf paper proves is that the first class cannot be made two-sided. The transport principle's founding move, resolving a nilpotent by a pair, is the first class, and the frozen point's passage from anti-de Sitter to de Sitter is the second, which is not a transport (Definition \claimref{obj.odd-extensions.single-extension}).
odd-extensions.two-classes-completion.technical:
Completions across a wall come in two classes. In the first, the same nondegenerate complement $K$ sits on both sides of the wall; then degeneracy is conserved and displaced to a shadow wall, and the ambient adjoins a hyperbolic plane to the whole bundle, of rank two by the minimal completion result and over the whole bundle because the standard complement must exist where the bundle is nondegenerate.

In the second class a family of hyperplanes in one fixed nondegenerate space is completed by a single line that changes type across the wall, of rank one; the $\Lambda$ family is completed this way. Nothing prevents a spacetime wall from being completed in the second class with a non-standard complement; what is proved is that the first class cannot be made two-sided. Resolving a nilpotent by a pair is of the first class, while the frozen point's passage from anti-de Sitter to de Sitter is of the second and is not a transport in the single-extension sense.
odd-extensions.two-classes-completion.lay: There are two different ways to complete a space whose metric degenerates along a wall. One keeps the same extra piece on both sides and adds a pair of directions everywhere; the other places the whole family inside one fixed larger space and adds a single direction whose character flips across the wall. The series' basic repair of division by zero is of the first kind. The passage from anti-de Sitter to de Sitter at the frozen point is of the second kind, and so is not a transport in the series' sense.

one-relation.imported-completion-ladder.formal: Division in a Clifford algebra fails exactly at the non-invertible elements, and among nondegenerate null-lift completions the minimal one adjoins one hyperbolic plane $(1,1)$; iterating gives the tower $\Cl(p+k, q+k) \cong \Mat(2^{k}, \Cl(p,q))$ with one fermionic mode adjoined per rung. For $p - q$ even the completed limit is $\Cl(p,q)_{\C} \otimes \mathrm{CAR}$, the ground algebra complexified and tensored with the CAR algebra; the odd-charge limit is open in the tower paper. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thm.~4.13]{ButlerT1}; \cite[Thm.~5.6, Question~5.8, Cor.~6.2]{ButlerT3}.
one-relation.imported-completion-ladder.technical:
Division in a Clifford algebra fails exactly at the non-invertible elements. Among nondegenerate null-lift completions the minimal one adjoins one hyperbolic plane of signature $(1,1)$, and iterating gives the tower $\Cl(p+k,q+k) \cong \Mat(2^k, \Cl(p,q))$, with one fermionic mode adjoined per rung.

For $p-q$ even the completed limit is $\Cl(p,q)_\C \otimes \CAR$, the complexified ground algebra tensored with the CAR algebra; the odd-charge limit is left open. The statement restates earlier series results.
one-relation.imported-completion-ladder.lay: Each time division fails, the smallest repair of the kind the series considers, a nondegenerate null-lift completion, adds one pair of directions, one of each sign, and repeating this builds an endless ladder of algebras, each a matrix algebra over the one below, with one new fermion-like mode per step. When the starting algebra has an even signature difference, the top of the ladder is the complexified starting algebra combined with the standard algebra of infinitely many fermion modes. The odd case is still open.

rule2.imported-completion-spacetime-alge.formal: The forced completion of the spacetime algebra is $\Cl(1,3) \hookrightarrow \Cl(2,4)$, and the complexified $\Cl(2,4)$ acts irreducibly on the Fock space of three fermionic ladder pairs, whose chirality halves are the conformal spinor space $\CS$ (Penrose's twistor space; in the real algebra it is the minimal left ideal $\Cl^+(2,4)P$, whose complex unit is $I_6$) and its conjugate dual. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thms.~4.2 and 4.13]{ButlerT1}; \cite[Thms.~3.1 and 3.4]{ButlerT9}.
rule2.imported-completion-spacetime-alge.technical:
The forced completion of the spacetime algebra is $\Cl(1,3) \hookrightarrow \Cl(2,4)$. The complexification of $\Cl(2,4)$ acts irreducibly on the Fock space of three fermionic ladder pairs, of complex dimension $2^3 = 8$, and the two chirality halves of that space are the conformal spinor space $\CS$, a minimal left ideal of the even algebra with complex unit $I_6$, and its conjugate dual.

The statement restates earlier series results.
rule2.imported-completion-spacetime-alge.lay: The smallest enlargement of the spacetime algebra that repairs division by zero adds two dimensions. Its spinors can be built like the states of three fermion modes, and splitting them by handedness gives exactly the four-dimensional spinors of conformal geometry, which Penrose found, and their dual.

rule2.imported-five-dimensional-chern-si.formal: A five-dimensional Dirac fermion of mass $m$ charged under a gauge field, integrated out, shifts the coefficient of the five-dimensional Chern-Simons term by $\tfrac12\sgn(m)$ (times the representation's cubic index for a non-abelian field); the sign is odd under the reflection of one spatial direction, so that the parity-violating term is present for a single species and absent for a pair whose contributions cancel. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Witten1996, IMS1997}.
rule2.imported-five-dimensional-chern-si.technical:
Integrating out a five-dimensional Dirac fermion of mass $m$ charged under a gauge field shifts the coefficient of the five-dimensional Chern-Simons term by $\tfrac12\sgn(m)$, times the cubic index of the representation for a non-abelian field.

The sign is odd under the reflection of one spatial direction, so the parity-violating term is present for a single species and absent for a pair whose contributions cancel. This is a standard result of five-dimensional gauge theory.
rule2.imported-five-dimensional-chern-si.lay: In five-dimensional theories, removing a heavy charged fermion from the description leaves behind a particular term for the gauge field, whose sign follows the sign of the fermion's mass. That term is not symmetric under mirror reflection, so a single such fermion breaks parity. A pair whose contributions cancel does not.

imported_from.citation: E. Witten, Phase transitions in M-theory and F-theory, Nucl. Phys. B 471 (1996) 195--216.
K. Intriligator, D. R. Morrison, N. Seiberg, Five-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theories and degenerations of Calabi-Yau spaces, Nucl. Phys. B 497 (1997) 56--100.

rule2.imported-graphenes-two-valleys-dou.formal: The low-energy theory of electrons on the honeycomb lattice consists of two two-component Dirac fermions, one at each of the two inequivalent corners $K, K'$ of the Brillouin zone, whose gamma matrices differ by the sign of one spatial gamma matrix; a lattice regularisation of a single two-component species is excluded by the fermion-doubling theorem, so the pair is forced. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Semenoff1984, NielsenNinomiya1981, GSC2007}.
rule2.imported-graphenes-two-valleys-dou.technical:
Near the two inequivalent corners $K$ and $K'$ of the Brillouin zone, electrons on the honeycomb lattice are described at low energy by two two-component Dirac fermions whose gamma matrices differ by the sign of one spatial gamma matrix.

The fermion-doubling theorem rules out a lattice regularisation of a single two-component species, so the pair is forced.
rule2.imported-graphenes-two-valleys-dou.lay: At low energies the electrons in graphene behave like two kinds of massless relativistic particles, one at each of two special points in momentum space. The two kinds are mirror images of each other along one direction. A general theorem about lattices says they must come as a pair, since a single kind cannot be put on a lattice.

imported_from.citation: G. W. Semenoff, Condensed-matter simulation of a three-dimensional anomaly, Phys. Rev. Lett. 53 (1984) 2449--2452.
H. B. Nielsen, M. Ninomiya, Absence of neutrinos on a lattice (I). Proof by homotopy theory, Nucl. Phys. B 185 (1981) 20--40.
V. P. Gusynin, S. G. Sharapov, J. P. Carbotte, AC conductivity of graphene: from tight-binding model to 2+1-dimensional quantum electrodynamics, Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 21 (2007) 4611--4658.

rule2.imported-parity-anomaly.formal: A single two-component Dirac fermion of mass $m$ in $2{+}1$ dimensions, coupled to a $U(1)$ gauge field, has an effective action containing a Chern-Simons term at level $\tfrac12\sgn(m)$ up to a sign that flips between the two inequivalent two-component representations; the term is odd under the reflection of one spatial axis, so a single species breaks parity, while two species, one in each representation with equal mass (equivalently the four-component fermion with its parity-invariant mass term), induce no net Chern-Simons term. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{NiemiSemenoff1983, Redlich1984, AGW1984}.
rule2.imported-parity-anomaly.technical:
A single two-component Dirac fermion of mass $m$ in $2+1$ dimensions, coupled to a $U(1)$ gauge field, has an effective action with a Chern-Simons term at level $\tfrac12\sgn(m)$, up to a sign that flips between the two inequivalent two-component representations.

The term is odd under the reflection of one spatial axis, so a single species breaks parity, while two species of equal mass, one in each representation (equivalently the four-component fermion with its parity-invariant mass term), induce no net Chern-Simons term.
rule2.imported-parity-anomaly.lay: In a flat two-dimensional world plus time, a single charged massive fermion leaves behind a term in the electromagnetic response that is not mirror-symmetric, so it breaks parity. Such fermions come in two mirror-image versions, which give this term with opposite signs. Taking one of each, with equal mass, cancels the effect.

imported_from.citation: A. J. Niemi, G. W. Semenoff, Axial-anomaly-induced fermion fractionization and effective gauge-theory actions in odd-dimensional space-times, Phys. Rev. Lett. 51 (1983) 2077--2080.

A. N. Redlich, Gauge noninvariance and parity nonconservation of three-dimensional fermions, Phys. Rev. Lett. 52 (1984) 18--21; Parity violation and gauge noninvariance of the effective gauge field action in three dimensions, Phys. Rev. D 29 (1984) 2366--2374.
L. Alvarez-Gaum'e, E. Witten, Gravitational anomalies, Nucl. Phys. B 234 (1984) 269--330.

rule2.imported-rule-2-matrix-units-forgo.lay: Some geometric algebras split into two separate halves that no internal symmetry can swap. Adding one new direction, of either sign, merges the halves into a single algebra in which swapping them becomes an internal operation. The merged algebra is the same whichever sign is chosen, so the algebra forgets that choice, and this merging happens at most once along any chain of repairs.
