rule2.rule-2-kaluza-klein-algebra.technical:
In $A_5 = \Cl(1,4)$ the volume element $\omega = \gamma e_4$, with $\gamma$ the spacetime pseudoscalar, is central with $\omega^2 = +1$, so $A_5 = \varepsilon_+A_5 \oplus \varepsilon_-A_5$ is of type C. Each ideal is a copy of $\Cl(1,3)$ through $a \mapsto \varepsilon_\pm a$, with $\varepsilon_\pm e_4 = \mp\varepsilon_\pm\gamma$, so the ideals are the two inequivalent five-dimensional Dirac representations $\Gamma^4 = \mp\Gamma^0\Gamma^1\Gamma^2\Gamma^3$ on the one Dirac spinor. The reflection $e_4 \mapsto -e_4$ is the automorphism $\hat{\cdot}\circ\mathrm{Ad}_{e_4}$; it exchanges the ideals and is outer.

The Rule 2 repairs are $\Cl(2,4)$, with $Q(
u) = +1$, and $\Cl(1,5)$, with $Q(
u) = -1$, both isomorphic to $\Mat_2(\Cl(1,3)) \cong \Mat_4(\HH)$ with $\varepsilon_\pm$ as diagonal matrix units. In either, conjugation by $
u$ is the grade involution of $A_5$ and conjugation by $
u e_4$ is the reflection, now inner: a boost in $\Cl(2,4)$, where $(
u e_4)^2 = +1$, and a rotation in $\Cl(1,5)$, where $(
u e_4)^2 = -1$. $\Cl(2,4)$ is the Rule 1 ascent of $\Cl(1,3)$, with $(
u, e_4)$ its hyperbolic plane and $	frac12(
u \pm e_4)$ its ladder pair; the residues run $6 	o 5 	o 6$ or $6 	o 5 	o 4$.
rule2.rule-2-kaluza-klein-algebra.lay: Adding a fifth dimension to spacetime, as in Kaluza-Klein theory, makes the geometric algebra split into two halves, which match the two inequivalent ways of writing a five-dimensional Dirac field. Reflecting the fifth direction swaps the halves, and nothing inside the algebra can perform that swap. Adding a sixth direction merges the halves and turns the reflection into an internal boost or rotation. With the sixth direction time-like, the merged algebra is the conformal algebra of spacetime, whose spinors are the four-dimensional spinors of conformal geometry.

The Rule 2 repairs are $\Cl(3,1)$, where $Q(
u) = +1$ is a third spatial direction, and $\Cl(2,2)$, where $Q(
u) = -1$ is a second time, both $\cong \Mat_4(\R)$. In them conjugation by $
u$ is the grade involution of $A_3$ and conjugation by $
u e_x$ is the planar reflection: a rotation in $\Cl(3,1)$ and a boost in $\Cl(2,2)$. $\Cl(3,1)$ is the Rule 1 ascent of $\Cl(2,0)$, with residues $2 	o 1 	o 2$ or $2 	o 1 	o 0$. rule2.rule-2-plane.lay: For a flat two-dimensional world plus time, with time given negative square, the geometric algebra splits into two halves, matching the two mirror-image kinds of two-component planar fermion. Reflecting one spatial axis swaps them, and this cannot be done from inside the algebra. Adding a third direction, either space-like or a second time, merges the halves and makes the reflection an internal rotation or boost. With the opposite sign convention for time the algebra does not split over the real numbers.

rule2.where-obstruction-sits-commuting-s.formal:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ with $n = p + q$ even, and let $A_s = \Cl(p,q{+}1)$ and $A_t = \Cl(p{+}1,q)$ be its spacelike and timelike one-dimensional extensions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Exactly one of $A_s$, $A_t$ carries the type-C obstruction: $A_s$ if $p - q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, $A_t$ if $p - q \equiv 0 \pmod 4$. The other has complex type: its volume element is central with square $-1$, its centre is $\C$, and it is simple.
\item[(b)] Each of the two ideals of the obstructed extension is a copy of $A$: $\varepsilon_\pm A_s \cong \Cl^0(p,q{+}1) \cong A$ in the first case, $\varepsilon_\pm A_t \cong \Cl^0(p{+}1,q) \cong \Cl(q,p) \cong A$ in the second (the last isomorphism because the residues $0$ and $4$ are fixed by negation mod $8$).
\item[(c)] The Rule 2 repair of the obstructed extension by a generator of the opposite sign is $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, the Rule 1 ascent of $A$: the two adjoined generators $e_{n+1}$ (the extension) and $\nu$ (the repair) span a hyperbolic plane, the null vectors $f = \tfrac12(\nu \pm e_{n+1})$, $f^* = \tfrac12(\nu \mp e_{n+1})$ (signs chosen so that each is null) are the ladder pair of Fact \claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}, and the two amplifications agree: $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(\text{extension})) = \Mat_2(A)$. The residue returns to $d$.
\item[(d)] The Rule 2 repair by a generator of the same sign is $\Cl(p,q{+}2)$ or $\Cl(p{+}2,q)$, isomorphic to $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ as an algebra, at residue $d \mp 2$; the adjoined plane is definite, carries no null vector, and admits no Rule 1 reading.
\end{enumerate}
rule2.where-obstruction-sits-commuting-s.technical:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ with $n = p + q$ even, and compare its two one-dimensional extensions, the spacelike $A_s = \Cl(p,q{+}1)$ and the timelike $A_t = \Cl(p{+}1,q)$. Exactly one of them carries the type-C obstruction: $A_s$ when $p - q \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ and $A_t$ when $p - q \equiv 0 \pmod 4$. The other is of complex type, with central volume element of square $-1$ and centre $\C$, and is simple. Each of the two ideals $\varepsilon_\pm$ of the obstructed extension is isomorphic to the even subalgebra of that extension, which is in turn a copy of $A$.

Repairing the obstructed extension by Rule 2 with a generator $
u$ of the opposite sign gives $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, the Rule 1 ascent of $A$: the extension direction $e_{n+1}$ and $
u$ span a hyperbolic plane, the null vectors $ rac12(
u \pm e_{n+1})$ form the Rule 1 ladder pair, and the two amplifications agree, $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(	ext{extension})) = \Mat_2(A)$, with the residue back at $d$. A repair by a generator of the same sign gives $\Cl(p,q{+}2)$ or $\Cl(p{+}2,q)$, isomorphic to $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ as an algebra but at residue $d \mp 2$; its adjoined plane is definite, has no null vector, and admits no Rule 1 reading.
rule2.where-obstruction-sits-commuting-s.lay: Take a geometry with an even number of dimensions and add one more direction, either of space or of time. Exactly one of the two choices produces an algebra that splits into two independent halves, and each half turns out to be a copy of the original algebra. Repairing that split by adding a further direction of the opposite kind lands on the same enlarged algebra as the series' other repair rule, so here the two rules agree. Adding a further direction of the same kind gives an algebra of the same shape, but it cannot be read as the other rule, because the added plane contains no light-like direction.

proofs.main:
(a) By Fact \claimref{rule2.imported-classification-centre-type-c}, an odd-dimensional algebra is type C exactly when $p' - q' \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and complex type exactly when $p' - q' \equiv 3 \pmod 4$; these exhaust the odd residues. For $A_s$, $p' - q' = p - q - 1$, which is $\equiv 1$ iff $p - q \equiv 2$ and $\equiv 3$ iff $p - q \equiv 0 \pmod 4$. For $A_t$, $p' - q' = p - q + 1$, which is $\equiv 1$ iff $p - q \equiv 0$ and $\equiv 3$ iff $p - q \equiv 2$. Since $n$ is even, $p - q$ is even, so exactly one case obtains for each extension and the two extensions fall on opposite sides. rungs.fact-null-momenta-invite-one-rung.formal: Let $p^{1}, \ldots, p^{n}$ be null vectors of $\R^{1,3} \subset \Cl(1,3)$, the momenta of $n$ massless conformal spinors (twistors). No extension of $\Cl(1,3)$ carries a $\mathrm{Spin}^{0}$-equivariant element-level inverse of the null vectors, so none inverts the $p^{i}$ in the sense the transport principle asks; the minimal completion that the transport principle prescribes is the single rung $\Cl(2,4)$, unique up to isometry and independent of $n$; and on that completion's quadric the transported reciprocal is total, sending every $p^{i}$ to its ideal point $[p^{i} + \tfrac12 n_{\infty}]$ at once. The transport principle completes the quadratic space, not each zero divisor: a second null momentum invites no second rung.
rungs.fact-null-momenta-invite-one-rung.technical:
Take $n$ null vectors $p^{1}, \ldots, p^{n}$ of $\R^{1,3} \subset \Cl(1,3)$, the momenta of $n$ massless conformal spinors, so $Q(p^{i}) = 0$. Applying the imported totality and minimality results to the quadratic space $(\R^{1,3}, \eta)$, which is nondegenerate of mixed signature, gives three conclusions at once. No extension of $\Cl(1,3)$ carries a $\mathrm{Spin}^{0}$-equivariant element-level inverse of the null vectors, so none inverts the $p^{i}$. The minimal completion is the single rung $\Cl(2,4)$, unique up to isometry and independent of $n$. On its quadric the transported reciprocal is total and sends every $p^{i}$ to its ideal point $[p^{i} + \frac12 \nInf]$ simultaneously.

The completion is a property of the quadratic space, whose null cone contains every $p^{i}$, and not of the individual zero divisors: a second null momentum does not call for a second rung.
rungs.fact-null-momenta-invite-one-rung.lay: Massless particles have momenta of zero length in spacetime, and such vectors cannot be divided by. The series' repair for this kind of failure adds one extra pair of dimensions, and this result notes that the same single addition deals with every such momentum at once. However many massless particles are present, one extra step, one rung, is enough, because the repair belongs to the geometry of spacetime rather than to any one particle.

proofs.main: All three clauses are Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-totality-minimality-completion} applied to $(\R^{1,3}, \eta)$, which is nondegenerate of mixed signature: the no-go for element-level inverses, the minimality and uniqueness of the one-plane completion, and the totality of the reciprocal on the quadric. The rung is determined by the quadratic space alone, whose null cone contains every $p^{i}$, and the reciprocal's totality is a statement about all null vectors of that cone simultaneously. A second conformal spinor changes the configuration, not the quadratic space. The corollary adds nothing to Fact \claimref{rungs.imported-totality-minimality-completion} beyond the observation that its hypotheses concern the quadratic space and not the number of null vectors named. The script confirms, in the blade engine, that a null $p$ stays null in $\Cl(2,4)$ and in $\Cl(3,5)$ (the rung is an isometric extension and inverts nothing as an element) and that the rungs supply one further anticommuting null pair each, orthogonal to $p$.

rungs.imported-totality-minimality-compl.formal: For a nondegenerate $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ of mixed signature and dimension $p + q \geq 3$, no extension of $\Cl(\mathbb{V})$ carries a $\mathrm{Spin}^{0}$-equivariant element-level inverse of the null vectors; the minimal null-lift completion is the adjunction of a single hyperbolic plane, $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, unique up to isometry, in every signature; and on that completion's quadric the transported reciprocal $\iota$ is total, continuous and involutive, agreeing with the geometric reciprocal on invertible vectors and sending every null vector $x_{0}$ to the ideal point $[x_{0} + \tfrac12 n_{\infty}]$, as the limit along every invertible path. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thms.~4.2, 4.10, 4.13]{ButlerT1}.
rungs.imported-totality-minimality-compl.technical:
For a nondegenerate quadratic space $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ of mixed signature with $p + q \geq 3$, three results of the root paper are taken together. First, no extension of $\Cl(\mathbb{V})$ carries a $\mathrm{Spin}^{0}$-equivariant element-level inverse of the null vectors. Second, the minimal null-lift completion adjoins a single hyperbolic plane, $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, unique up to isometry in every signature.

Third, on that completion's quadric the transported reciprocal $\iota$ is total, continuous and involutive, agrees with the geometric reciprocal on invertible vectors, and sends every null vector $x_{0}$, with $Q(x_{0}) = 0$, to the ideal point $[x_{0} + \frac12 \nInf]$, which is also the limit along every invertible path.
rungs.imported-totality-minimality-compl.lay: This collects three results from the series' founding paper for use in a later note. Vectors of zero length cannot be inverted in any symmetric way, however the algebra is enlarged. But adding exactly one extra pair of dimensions, one of positive and one of negative square, makes the reciprocal defined everywhere on the space of points, and a zero-length vector is then sent to a definite point at infinity.

singularity.transport-schwarzschild-fibr.formal:
Fix $p$ in the invertible region of the Schwarzschild gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), take $T_pM$ to be the background vectors at $p$, and write $Q_p(x) := Q(\hb^{-1}(x))$ for the square of the physical vector over $x$ and $Q^*_p(\xi) := Q(\hb^{T}(\xi))$ for the dual norm of a covector. Vectors and covectors are read in the physical space: the gauge field carries the flat background to the physical vectors, a vector $x$ to $\hb^{-1}(x)$ and a covector $\xi$ to $\hb^{T}(\xi)$, the lift $X_p(x)$ carries $\hb^{-1}(x)$ in its vector slot, and the values in (2) to (4) are taken through this identification ($x/Q_p(x)$ is the physical vector $\hb^{-1}(x)/Q_p(x)$, $x + \tfrac12 \nInf$ is $\hb^{-1}(x) + \tfrac12 \nInf$, and $\xi/r$ is $\hb^{T}(\xi)/r$). In the static gauge the Gram of $Q_p$ is the derived metric $g_p = \operatorname{diag}(f, -f^{-1}, -r^2, -r^2\sin^2\theta)$ with $f = 1 - 2M/r$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $X_p(x)$ satisfies the incidence condition for every $x \in T_pM$, and $\iota$ preserves it and is an involution.
\item[(2)] \emph{(Invertible directions: the transport returns to the original space.)} If $Q_p(x) \neq 0$ then $\dsc\bigl(\iota(X_p(x))\bigr) = x/Q_p(x)$, the classical reciprocal.
\item[(3)] \emph{(Null directions: the transport does not return.)} If $Q_p(x) = 0$, that is if $x$ is physically null, in particular for the radial null direction $x = \et + f\,\er$, then $\iota(X_p(x)) = [\,x + \tfrac12 \nInf\,]$, an ideal point, and $\dsc$ is undefined on it.
\item[(4)] \emph{(The dying direction, and where the descent fails.)} Let $\xi := k = \sqrt r\,dr + \sqrt{2M}\,dt_{\mathrm{PG}}$ be the generator of the radical line of the degeneration in the weighted Painlev\'e-Gullstrand coframe of \cite[Thm.~8.7]{ButlerT4}, in the static chart $\xi = \sqrt{2M}\,dt_s + (\sqrt r/f)\,dr$. Its dual norm is $Q^*_p(\xi) = -r$ exactly, at every radius, the horizon included: nonzero for every $r > 0$ and tending to $0$ as $r \to 0^+$. Consequently $\iota(X_p(\xi))$ descends at every point $r > 0$, to $\dsc = -\xi/r$, and converges, as $r \to 0^+$, to an ideal point at which $\dsc$ is undefined. The read-out fails exactly on $E$ and nowhere else in the physical closure.
\end{enumerate}
singularity.transport-schwarzschild-fibr.technical:
Fix a point $p$ in the invertible region of the Schwarzschild gravitational field on flat spacetime, whose gauge field $\hb$ carries the flat background to the physical vectors (a vector $x$ to $\hb^{-1}(x)$, a covector $\xi$ to $\hb^{T}(\xi)$), with $Q_p(x) = Q(\hb^{-1}(x))$ the square of the physical vector over the background vector $x$, whose Gram in the static gauge is the derived metric $g_p = \operatorname{diag}(f, -f^{-1}, -r^2, -r^2\sin^2\theta)$ with $f = 1 - 2M/r$, and lift $x \in T_pM$ through its physical vector, $X_p(x) = (1, \hb^{-1}(x), \frac12 Q_p(x))$, in the homogeneous coordinates $(s, x, t)$ of the completion $\Cl(2,4)$. Every lift satisfies the incidence condition $Q_p(x) = 2st$, and the transported reciprocal $\iota(s,x,t) = (2t, x, \frac12 s)$ preserves it and is an involution. If $Q_p(x) \neq 0$ the read-out returns the classical reciprocal, $\dsc(\iota(X_p(x))) = \hb^{-1}(x)/Q_p(x)$, the physical vector over $x/Q_p(x)$. If $Q_p(x) = 0$, for instance on the radial null direction $\et + f\,\er$, the image is the ideal point $[\hb^{-1}(x) + \frac12 \nInf]$ and $\dsc$ is undefined there.

For the generator $\xi = \sqrt{2M}\,dt_s + (\sqrt r/f)\,dr$ of the radical line of the degeneration, taken from the weighted Painlev\'e-Gullstrand coframe, the dual norm, the derived cometric $Q^{*}_p(\xi) = Q(\hb^{T}(\xi))$, is exactly $-r$ at every radius, the horizon included. Hence $\iota(X_p(\xi))$ descends to $\dsc = -\hb^{T}(\xi)/r$, the physical covector over $-\xi/r$, at every $r > 0$ and converges, as $r \to 0^{+}$, to an ideal point at which $\dsc$ is undefined: the read-out fails exactly on $E$ and nowhere else in the physical closure.
singularity.transport-schwarzschild-fibr.lay: At each point of a non-rotating black hole away from its centre, the series' repair is carried out explicitly on the space of directions. Ordinary directions go up into the enlarged space and come back down as their usual reciprocals, while light-like directions go up to points at infinity that have nothing below them. The one direction that dies at the singularity can be brought back down at every radius, however close to the centre, and fails to come back only in the limit at the centre itself. So the read-out breaks down exactly at the singularity and nowhere else, the horizon included.

proofs.main:
Here $Q_p(x) = Q(\hb^{-1}(x))$ and $Q^*_p(\xi) = Q(\hb^{T}(\xi))$, the derived metric and cometric of the gravitational field at $p$, whose static-gauge Grams are those displayed (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}(i)). (1) With $X_p(x) = (1, x, \tfrac12 Q_p(x))$ (the triples of \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form}) the incidence condition reads $Q_p(x) = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot \tfrac12 Q_p(x)$, an identity. Applying $\iota$ gives $(Q_p(x), x, \tfrac12)$, whose incidence check is $2 \cdot Q_p(x) \cdot \tfrac12 = Q_p(x)$, again an identity; and $\iota^2(s,x,t) = \iota(2t, x, \tfrac12 s) = (s, x, t)$.

(2) $\iota(X_p(x)) = (Q_p(x), x, \tfrac12)$, so $\dsc$ returns $x/Q_p(x)$, which is the classical reciprocal $\rho(x)$ of \cite[Lem.~4.23(2)]{ButlerT1} (\claimref{transport.descent-read-out-map}).

(3) For the stated $x$, $Q_p(x) = f \cdot 1 - f^{-1} \cdot f^2 = f - f = 0$, so $X_p(x) = (1, x, 0)$ and $\iota(X_p(x)) = (0, x, \tfrac12)$: the first slot vanishes, which is the defining condition of an ideal point, and $\dsc$ requires division by it. The value is $[\,x + \tfrac12 \nInf\,]$, exactly the ideal value of \cite[Thm.~4.10(3)]{ButlerT1} (\claimref{transport.totality}).

(4) With $t_{\mathrm{PG}} = t_s + \int \beta f^{-1}dr$ and $\beta^{2} = 2M/r$, $dt_{\mathrm{PG}} = dt_s + (\beta/f)dr$, so $k = \sqrt{2M}\,dt_s + \sqrt r\,(1 + 2M/rf)\,dr = \sqrt{2M}\,dt_s + (\sqrt r/f)\,dr$, using $f + 2M/r = 1$. In the static cometric $(g_p^{-1})^{tt} = 1/f$, $(g_p^{-1})^{rr} = -f$, so $Q^*_p(\xi) = 2M/f - f\,(r/f^{2}) = (2M - r)/f = -r$, an identity of rational functions in $r$ with no pole at the horizon; in the Painlev\'e-Gullstrand frame of \cite[Thm.~8.7]{ButlerT4} (\claimref{sheaf.schwarzschild-degeneration-boundary-tame}) the same value is read off the polynomial Gram matrix as $g_k = (m^{2} - r) - 2m^{2} + m^{2} = -r$ with $m = \sqrt{2M}$, which is that theorem's clause (3). Hence $\iota(X_p(\xi)) = (-r, \xi, \tfrac12)$ has nonvanishing first slot at every $r > 0$, where $\dsc$ returns $-\xi/r$, and first slot tending to $0$ as $r \to 0^+$, which is the ideal stratum. (The Killing-time covector $dt_s$ itself, with $Q^*_p(dt_s) = 1/f$, spans the radical line only on $E$ \cite[Thm.~8.7(4)]{ButlerT4}, and its static norm has a pole at the horizon where nothing degenerates; $k$ is the regular generator.) One further line closes the junction with Step 1, computed in the Painlev\'e-Gullstrand chart where Propositions \claimref{singularity.cones-fold} and \claimref{singularity.degeneration-exactly} fold the cones: the PG cometric has $g^{tt} = 1$, $g^{tr} = -\beta$, $g^{rr} = \beta^{2} - 1$, so for $k = \sqrt{2M}\,dt_{\mathrm{PG}} + \sqrt r\,dr$ the dual's $t$-component is $\sqrt{2M} - \beta\sqrt r = 0$ identically and its $r$-component is $-\beta\sqrt{2M} + (\beta^{2} - 1)\sqrt r = -\sqrt r$: $k^{\sharp} = -\sqrt r\,\er$ exactly, at every radius and with no horizon pole, in the same frame as Step 1, so the corank-one radical of the completion and Step 1's dying direction $\er$ are the same direction outright, not merely in the limit. That the failure locus is exactly $E$, and that no shadow wall forms elsewhere, is \cite[Thm.~8.12]{ButlerT4} (\claimref{sheaf.one-sided-completion-singularity}). All identities in (1) to (4) are machine-verified in exact symbolic arithmetic (the section “Machine verification”, parts L1 to L14), and the nullity of the lift, $X_p(x)^{2} = 0$ in $\Cl(2,4)$ with the stated normalisation, blade-exactly.

synthesis.imported-invariant-cone-classi.formal: Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional simple real Lie algebra with Cartan decomposition $\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{k} \oplus \mathfrak{p}$, $\mathfrak{k}$ a maximal compact subalgebra. Then $\mathfrak{g}$ contains a closed convex cone $W$, invariant under the adjoint group ($e^{\mathrm{ad}X}W = W$ for all $X \in \mathfrak{g}$), with $W \neq \{0\}$ and $W \neq \mathfrak{g}$, if and only if the centre $\mathfrak{z}(\mathfrak{k})$ is nonzero, that is, if and only if $\mathfrak{g}$ is of hermitian type. (For simple $\mathfrak{g}$ such a cone is automatically pointed and generating: $W \cap -W$ and $W - W$ are invariant subspaces, hence ideals, so they are $\{0\}$ and $\mathfrak{g}$.) \emph{Provenance:} Kostant (reported in \cite{Segal1976}); \cite{Vinberg1980, Paneitz1981, Paneitz1983, Olshanskii1981, Olshanskii1982}.
synthesis.imported-invariant-cone-classi.technical: A simple real Lie algebra admits a nontrivial closed convex cone invariant under its adjoint group exactly when it is of hermitian type, which means that the centre of its maximal compact subalgebra is nonzero (equivalently, the corresponding symmetric space is a bounded symmetric domain). For a simple algebra any nonzero proper invariant closed convex cone is pointed and spans the algebra, because its edge and its span are ideals. The theory was begun by Kostant, Segal and Vinberg; the classification is due to Vinberg, Paneitz and Ol'shanskii.
synthesis.imported-invariant-cone-classi.lay: In a symmetry algebra, an invariant cone is a set of directions closed under adding and under every symmetry transformation, which picks out a consistent notion of 'positive'. A classical theorem of Lie theory says that a simple symmetry algebra has such a cone, other than the trivial ones, exactly when it contains a special rotation that commutes with all its other rotations. This is a known result taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: E. B. Vinberg, Invariant convex cones and orderings in Lie groups, Funct. Anal. Appl. 14 (1980), 1--10.

synthesis.positive-energy-selects-rule-2.formal:
Let the base be the spacetime algebra $\Cl(1,3)$, or its mirror $\Cl(3,1)$. By Theorem \claimref{rule2.where-obstruction-sits-commuting-square}(a) its obstructed one-dimensional extension is $\Cl(p,q{+}1)$ in either case ($\Cl(1,4)$, resp. $\Cl(3,2)$), and by (c) and (d) the two Rule 2 repairs are the opposite-sign repair, the Rule 1 ascent $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ ($\Cl(2,4)$, resp. $\Cl(4,2)$, both with $\nu^{2} = +1$), and the same-sign repair $\Cl(p,q{+}2)$ ($\Cl(1,5)$, resp. $\Cl(3,3)$, both with $\nu^{2} = -1$). Write $\so(p,q) = \mathfrak{k} \oplus \mathfrak{p}$ for the Cartan decomposition by the bivectors $e_{i}e_{j}$, rotations ($(e_{i}e_{j})^{2} = -1$) spanning $\mathfrak{k}$ and boosts spanning $\mathfrak{p}$. Call a continuous unitary representation $\pi$ of $\mathrm{Spin}(p,q)$ \emph{of positive energy} if it is nontrivial on the identity component $\mathrm{Spin}^{+}(p,q)$ and some nonzero element $X$ of the Lie algebra acts by a generator $-I_{4}\,d\pi(X)$ that is bounded below (the spectrum condition), the Hilbert space's scalars read in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$, the default scalar field of an abstract complex Hilbert space.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] (Exact.) The centre of $\mathfrak{k}$ is one-dimensional for $\so(2,4)$ and $\so(4,2)$, and zero for $\so(1,5)$, $\so(3,3)$ and the base $\so(1,3)$. It is spanned by the rotation $Z$ of the plane of the two generators that square alike and are in the minority: the base time direction and whichever of the extension generator and $\nu$ squares like time. In $\Cl(2,4)$ that is $Z = e_{0}\nu$; in $\Cl(4,2)$ it is the time direction times the extension generator, while there $e_{0}\nu$ is a boost. In each case $Z^{2} = -1$ and $\mathrm{ad}(Z)^{2} = -4$ on $\mathfrak{p}$, so $\tfrac12\mathrm{ad}(Z)$ is a complex structure on $\mathfrak{p}$.
\item[(ii)] (Existence.) $\mathrm{Spin}^{+}(2,4) \cong SU(2,2)$ has representations of positive energy: the series constructs them in the twistor attachment (Proposition \claimref{field-theory.twistor-attachment}), where the conformal energy on the helicity-$s$ module is $|s| + 1 + n$. That this energy is generated by the central rotation $Z$ of (i) (the conformal Hamiltonian) is the standard identification, argued and not proved here; existence does not depend on it.
\item[(iii)] (Non-existence, by one import.) By the classification of invariant cones (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-invariant-cone-classification}: a simple real Lie algebra contains a closed invariant convex cone other than $0$ and itself exactly when the centre of its maximal compact subalgebra is nonzero), neither $\mathrm{Spin}(1,5)$ nor $\mathrm{Spin}(3,3)$ has a representation of positive energy.
\end{enumerate}
So, with that imported classification, the spectrum condition imposed on the symmetry group of the completed algebra admits the opposite-sign repair, the Rule 1 ascent $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, and excludes the same-sign one, in both signature conventions; for our tower it returns $\Cl(2,4)$, where $\nu$ is a second direction squaring like time and pairs with $e_{0}$ into the compact central plane. The selection is by a physical requirement on the dynamics (a generator bounded below), not by the representation theory of the fermions, and it is a condition on the spin group built from a chosen vector slot rather than a property of the abstract fused algebra; it is not derived from equations of motion.
synthesis.positive-energy-selects-rule-2.technical:
The two Rule 2 repairs of the obstructed extension of the spacetime algebra differ only in the sign of the adjoined generator: $\Cl(2,4)$ for $
u^{2} = +1$ and $\Cl(1,5)$ for $
u^{2} = -1$ (in the mirror convention $\Cl(4,2)$ for $
u^{2} = +1$ and $\Cl(3,3)$ for $
u^{2} = -1$). As algebras they are isomorphic, but their bivector Lie algebras are different real forms of $\so(6,\C)$: $\so(2,4) \cong \su(2,2)$, while $\so(1,5) \cong \mathfrak{sl}(2,\HH)$ and $\so(3,3) \cong \mathfrak{sl}(4,\R)$.

The difference that matters physically is whether the group can act with positive energy. By the imported invariant-cone classification, a simple real Lie algebra has a nontrivial unitary representation with a generator bounded below only when its maximal compact subalgebra has a centre; the remaining step, that a representation with all generators bounded is trivial on the identity component, is proved here by a scaling argument. The exact computation finds that centre one-dimensional for $\so(2,4)$ and $\so(4,2)$, spanned by the rotation of the base time direction with whichever new generator squares like time, with $	frac12\mathrm{ad}(Z)$ a complex structure on the boosts; for $\so(1,5)$ and $\so(3,3)$ it is zero. The series' twistor attachment already realises positive-energy representations of $SU(2,2)$.

So, with the imported classification, imposing the spectrum condition on the completion's symmetry selects the Rule 1 ascent, $
u^{2} = +1$ in both conventions; in the $\Cl(1,3)$ convention the repair direction pairs with time into a compact plane, the conformal-time circle. The same invariant cone underlies the causal order of compactified Minkowski space, so positivity of energy and causal order read one structure two ways. The classification is the one step taken from outside the series.
synthesis.positive-energy-selects-rule-2.lay: To finish building its basic algebra the series must add one extra direction, and the mathematics alone does not say which of two signs that direction carries. Both choices give the same algebra on paper. This result asks a physical question instead: can the resulting symmetry act on quantum states with an energy that never runs to minus infinity? A theorem from the theory of Lie groups, taken from the literature, says that this is possible only when the symmetry contains a special rotation that commutes with all the other rotations. An exact computation shows that such a rotation exists only for the series' choice of sign; in the series' usual conventions it is the rotation that carries ordinary time into the new direction. So, given that theorem, the requirement that energy be bounded below picks the series' choice. The one step taken from outside the series is that Lie-group theorem.

proofs.main:
\emph{Step 1 (the two repairs).} For $A = \Cl(1,3)$, $p - q = -2 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, so by Theorem \claimref{rule2.where-obstruction-sits-commuting-square}(a) the spacelike extension $\Cl(1,4)$ is obstructed, and by (c) and (d) its Rule 2 repairs are $\Cl(2,4)$ (adjoined $
u$ of the opposite sign, $
u^{2} = +1$, the adjoined plane hyperbolic) and $\Cl(1,5)$ ($
u^{2} = -1$, the adjoined plane definite). For the mirror $\Cl(3,1)$, $p - q = 2$, the obstructed extension is again $\Cl(p,q{+}1) = \Cl(3,2)$ (in this convention its new generator squares like time), with repairs $\Cl(4,2)$ ($
u^{2} = +1$, opposite sign, the Rule 1 ascent) and $\Cl(3,3)$ ($
u^{2} = -1$, same sign). The check recomputes these four signatures from the rule of (a).

\emph{Step 2 (the Cartan decomposition and its centre).} In $\Cl(p,q)$ the bivectors $e_{i}e_{j}$, $i < j$, span a Lie algebra under the commutator isomorphic to $\so(p,q)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.bivector-lie-algebra}). Since $(e_{i}e_{j})^{2} = -e_{i}^{2}e_{j}^{2}$, a bivector squares to $-1$ when its two factors square alike and to $+1$ otherwise; the first kind span $\mathfrak{k} \cong \so(p) \oplus \so(q)$, the maximal compact subalgebra (for $(2,4)$ of dimension $7$, matching the $SO(2) 	imes SO(4)$ of Fact \claimref{standard-model.imported-maximal-compact-subgroups}), and the second span $\mathfrak{p}$. The centre of $\mathfrak{k}$ is the kernel of the linear map $X \mapsto ([X, k])_{k \in \mathfrak{k}}$ on $\mathfrak{k}$; the check computes its rank over $\Q$ and finds kernel dimension $1$ for $(2,4)$ and $(4,2)$ and $0$ for $(1,5)$ and $(3,3)$. By hand: $\so(p) \oplus \so(q)$ has centre $\so(2)$ for each factor with index $2$ and nothing from factors with index $1$ or at least $3$, which gives the same four values. For $(2,4)$ the central element is $Z = e_{0}
u$, the product of the two generators squaring $+1$, that is of the spacetime time direction and the repair generator; it commutes with every rotation, and the check verifies $Z^{2} = -1$ and $[Z,[Z,x]] = -4x$ for every boost $x$, so $J = 	frac12\mathrm{ad}(Z)$ satisfies $J^{2} = -1$ on $\mathfrak{p}$ (the Hermitian-type structure). In $\Cl(4,2)$ the two generators squaring $-1$ are the base time direction and the extension generator, their product is the central rotation, and $e_{\mathrm{time}}
u$ is a boost, $(e_{\mathrm{time}}
u)^{2} = +1$ (also checked); so the identification of the central plane as the plane of time and $
u$ holds in the $\Cl(1,3)$ convention only, while in both conventions it is the plane of time and the new generator squaring like time. In $\Cl(1,5)$ the plane of $e_{0}$ and $
u$ has $(e_{0}
u)^{2} = -e_{0}^{2}
u^{2} = +1$: it is a boost plane, and the check confirms that every rotation fails to commute with some other rotation, so no rotation is central.

\emph{Step 3 (existence for the opposite-sign repair).} Proposition \claimref{field-theory.twistor-attachment} constructs, on the conformal spinor space with its $\mathfrak{u}(2,2)$ action, positive-energy modules: the helicity-$s$ module has energies $|s| + 1 + n$, bounded below by $|s| + 1$, so $\mathrm{Spin}^{+}(2,4) \cong SU(2,2)$ has representations of positive energy. That the conformal energy is the compact generator spanning the $\so(2)$ centre of $\mathfrak{k}$ in Step 2 (the conformal Hamiltonian $	frac12(P_{0} + K_{0})$ in the usual notation) is the standard identification; the store does not state it, and it is argued here, not proved. Existence does not depend on it.

\emph{Step 4 (non-existence for the same-sign repair, given the import).} Let $\pi$ be a representation of positive energy of $G = \mathrm{Spin}(p,q)$ with $\mathfrak{g} = \so(p,q)$ simple and noncompact, and let $C_{\pi} = \{X \in \mathfrak{g} : -I_{4}\,d\pi(X) 	ext{ is bounded below}\}$ (scalars in $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{4}\}$). It is invariant under $\mathrm{Ad}(G)$ (conjugation by $\pi(g)$ preserves semiboundedness) and is a convex cone (a sum of two operators bounded below is bounded below on the common domain of smooth vectors). It is not $0$, by hypothesis. It is not all of $\mathfrak{g}$. Otherwise $X$ and $-X$ both lie in it for every $X$, so every $d\pi(X)$ is bounded. Since $\mathfrak{g}$ has real rank at least one, it contains $H, E$ with $[H, E] = 2E$ and $E 
eq 0$; unitarity gives $\|d\pi(E)\| = \|\pi(e^{tH})d\pi(E)\pi(e^{-tH})\| = \|d\pi(\mathrm{Ad}(e^{tH})E)\| = e^{2t}\|d\pi(E)\|$ for every real $t$, so $d\pi(E) = 0$. The kernel of $d\pi$ is then a nonzero ideal of the simple $\mathfrak{g}$, hence all of $\mathfrak{g}$, and $\pi$ is trivial on the identity component, against the definition. Its closure is a closed invariant convex cone, and it is not $\mathfrak{g}$ either, since a convex set in a finite-dimensional space has the same interior as its closure, so a dense $C_{\pi}$ would be all of $\mathfrak{g}$. The imported classification (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-invariant-cone-classification}) states that a simple real Lie algebra contains a closed invariant convex cone other than $0$ and $\mathfrak{g}$ only if it is of Hermitian type, that is only if the centre of its maximal compact subalgebra is nonzero. By Step 2, $\so(1,5)$ and $\so(3,3)$ are not of Hermitian type. Hence $\mathrm{Spin}(1,5)$ and $\mathrm{Spin}(3,3)$ have no representation of positive energy. (The requirement of nontriviality on the identity component is needed: these groups are disconnected, and a representation through the component group alone has $d\pi = 0$.)

\emph{Step 5 (conclusion and scope).} Imposing the spectrum condition on the symmetry group of the completed algebra therefore admits $
u^{2} = +1$ (the Rule 1 ascent) and excludes $
u^{2} = -1$ for the spacetime algebra and for its mirror, given the import of Step 4. The principle is a requirement on the dynamics (its generator is bounded below), not a statement about the fermion representations; it is not derived here from equations of motion, and the series must still take the spectrum condition as given, as its twistor attachment already does. The base Lorentz algebra $\so(1,3)$ has zero centre in $\mathfrak{k}$ (also checked), so the discrimination appears only after the completion. Labels: Steps 1 and 2 are proved and checked exactly; Step 3 is the store's proved construction; Step 3's identification of the energy generator is argued (standard); Step 4 is proved from the one named import, Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-invariant-cone-classification}.

synthesis.rule-2-fusing-plane-lorentzian.technical:
Rule 2 repairs the split extension $\Cl(1,4)$ by one more generator $
u$ whose square, $+1$ (giving $\Cl(2,4)$) or $-1$ (giving $\Cl(1,5)$), the fused algebra forgets. This result finds where the bit sits. Inside the fused algebra, the elements that anticommute with all five generators of the extension form a plane spanned by $
u$ and the volume element $\Omega$; the square is a quadratic form on it, and it is Lorentzian for either choice, because $
u$ and $\Omega$ always square to opposite signs. The plane's two null lines are the Rule 2 matrix units $
u\varepsilon_{\pm}$, the zero divisors that fuse the two ideals.

Any unit vector of that plane completes the extension's generators to a generating set of the whole algebra, of signature $(2,4)$ or $(1,5)$ by the sign of its square, and the volume element of that completion is the orthogonal axis, with the opposite square. So one algebra contains both repairs, and the isomorphism between them that fixes the extension exchanges the new vector with the volume element. The automorphisms fixing the extension act on the plane as boosts and their negatives, transitively on each sign and never across. A principle that sees only the fused algebra and the extension cannot choose; one that chooses must say which element is a vector. The spectrum condition on the completion's spin group, the result filed alongside, synthesis.positive-energy-selects-rule-2-sign, is a selector of that kind: it is a condition on the group built from the chosen vector slot, not on the abstract algebra. The series' choice $\Cl(2,4)$ is equivalent to the volume element, the other axis, squaring to $-1$, which makes it the complex unit of the even algebra; this is the residue modulo four already in the store, restated, not a dynamical derivation.
synthesis.rule-2-fusing-plane-lorentzian.lay: When the series' fourth step glues two halves of an algebra back together, it adds one new direction whose type, time-like or space-like, the resulting algebra cannot remember. This result shows where that missing bit lives. Inside the glued algebra, the directions that could do the gluing form a flat two-dimensional plane that has the geometry of a spacetime with one time and one space axis, whichever choice was made. Its light-like lines are the special elements that do the gluing. Picking the new direction time-like gives the series' conformal algebra; picking it space-like gives the alternative. In both cases the axis not picked becomes the algebra's built-in imaginary unit or its opposite. So nothing inside the glued algebra can make the choice; it has to come from outside.

transport.ascent-renders-grade-involutio.formal:
Let $\gamma = \pm 1$. Conjugation by $
u$ in $B_\gamma$ restricts on $A$ to the grade involution:
\[

u\, a\, 
u^{-1} \;=\; \hat{a} \qquad (a \in A).
\]
In particular $
u \omega 
u^{-1} = -\omega$ and $
u \varepsilon_\pm 
u^{-1} = \varepsilon_\mp$: the two formerly central projectors become an inner-conjugate pair. Consequently the two-sided ideal of $B_\gamma$ generated by either projector is all of $B_\gamma$, by the one-line computation
\[
\varepsilon_+ \;+\; 
u\,\varepsilon_+\,
u^{-1} \;=\; \varepsilon_+ + \varepsilon_- \;=\; 1 .
\]
The obstruction of Remark \claimref{note.transport.typec-depth} is thereby resolved in the exact sense there identified: the symmetry exchanging the two ideals, outer on the split algebra, is inner in the ascent, and its availability is what fuses them.
transport.ascent-renders-grade-involutio.technical:
In the one-generator ascent $B_\gamma$ of $A$, with adjoined generator $
u$ of $Q(
u) = \gamma = \pm 1$, conjugation by $
u$ restricts on $A$ to the grade involution: $
u\, a\, 
u^{-1} = \hat a$. Since the volume element $\omega$ has odd grade, $
u\omega
u^{-1} = -\omega$, so the formerly central projectors are exchanged, $
u \varepsilon_\pm 
u^{-1} = \varepsilon_\mp$, and become an inner-conjugate pair.

Consequently the two-sided ideal of $B_\gamma$ generated by either projector is all of $B_\gamma$, because $\varepsilon_+ + 
u\varepsilon_+
u^{-1} = \varepsilon_+ + \varepsilon_- = 1$. The symmetry exchanging the two ideals, outer on the split algebra, is inner in the ascent, and its availability is what fuses them.
transport.ascent-renders-grade-involutio.lay: Some Clifford algebras split into two independent halves, and the symmetry that swaps the halves cannot be produced from inside the algebra. Adding one new direction changes that: conjugating by the new direction performs the swap. Once the swap is available inside the algebra, the two halves can no longer be kept apart, and they merge into one.

transport.conformal-gram-matrix.formal:
Fix an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of $\mathbb{V}$ and the $n + 2$ points
\[
p_0 = 0, \qquad p_i = e_i \ (1 \leq i \leq n), \qquad p_{n+1} = 2e_1 .
\]
Then the symmetric $(n{+}2) \times (n{+}2)$ matrix $M_{ij} = -\tfrac12 Q(p_i - p_j)$ has rank $n + 2$ and signature $(p{+}1,\, q{+}1)$.
transport.conformal-gram-matrix.technical:
Take an orthogonal basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of $\mathbb{V}$ and the $n + 2$ points $p_0 = 0$, $p_i = e_i$ for $1 \leq i \leq n$, and $p_{n+1} = 2e_1$. The symmetric $(n{+}2) \times (n{+}2)$ matrix $M_{ij} = -\frac12 Q(p_i - p_j)$ then has full rank $n + 2$ and signature $(p{+}1, q{+}1)$.

So a table built only from separations in the original space already has the rank and signature of the completed space two dimensions up.
transport.conformal-gram-matrix.lay: Pick a few specific points in a space: the origin, one unit step along each axis, and a point two steps along the first axis. Write down a table of their squared separations, halved and with the sign reversed. Read as a quadratic form, that table has exactly one more positive and one more negative direction than the original space.
transport.conformal-gram-matrix.typing_note: No premises: the proof is a direct computation using the model identity of the conformal lift, which is an equation of the paper rather than a store claim.

transport.descent-read-out-map.formal:
Define $\dsc : \mathcal{Q} \setminus \{\text{ideal points}\} \to \mathbb{V}$ by
\[
\dsc\,[\, s\,\nO + x + t\,\nInf \,] \;=\; x/s .
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\dsc$ is well defined and continuous, and it is inverse to the lift: $\dsc[X(x)] = x$ for every $x \in \mathbb{V}$, and $X(\dsc[N]) \in [N]$ for every non-ideal null ray $[N]$. Hence $x \mapsto [X(x)]$ and $\dsc$ are mutually inverse homeomorphisms between $\mathbb{V}$ and $\mathcal{Q} \setminus \{\text{ideal points}\}$.
\item On the invertible locus, descent returns the classical reciprocal: for every $x$ with $Q(x) \neq 0$,
\[
\dsc\bigl(\iota[X(x)]\bigr) \;=\; x/Q(x) \;=\; \rho(x).
\]
\item The composite $\dsc \circ \iota \circ [X(\cdot)]$ is defined exactly on $\{Q \neq 0\}$: for $Q(x_0) = 0$ the value $\iota[X(x_0)]$ is ideal by Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}(3) and lies outside the domain of $\dsc$. Descent is therefore partial precisely where the original reciprocal was, and necessarily so, since the ideal points are represented by no point of $\mathbb{V}$.
\end{enumerate}
transport.descent-read-out-map.technical:
The read-out $\dsc[\, s\,
O + x + t\,
Inf \,] = x/s$ is defined on the quadric minus its ideal points, those with $s = 0$. It is well defined, continuous and inverse to the lift: $\dsc[X(x)] = x$, and $X(\dsc[N]) \in [N]$ for every non-ideal null ray, so the lift and $\dsc$ are mutually inverse homeomorphisms between $\mathbb{V}$ and the non-ideal part of $\mathcal{Q}$.

On the invertible locus, lifting, applying the transported reciprocal $\iota$ and reading out returns the classical reciprocal: $\dsc(\iota[X(x)]) = x/Q(x)$. The composite is defined exactly where $Q(x) 
eq 0$; for $Q(x_0) = 0$, totality places $\iota[X(x_0)]$ at an ideal point, outside the domain of $\dsc$. Descent is therefore partial precisely where the original reciprocal was, and necessarily so, since ideal points are represented by no point of $\mathbb{V}$.
transport.descent-read-out-map.lay: After computing in the enlarged space one needs a way back to the original one. The read-out map does this for every point not at infinity, and for ordinary invertible vectors it gives back the familiar reciprocal. For zero-length vectors the answer lies at infinity, and the read-out declines, because no point of the original space represents it.
transport.descent-read-out-map.typing_note: Kept the single premise, totality, used for clauses (2) and (3); the incidence condition the proof cites is an equation, not a store claim.

proofs.main:
(1) Scaling a representative by $\lambda \neq 0$ scales $s$ and $x$ alike, so $x/s$ is unchanged and $\dsc$ is well defined; the map $N \mapsto x(N)/s(N)$ is continuous on the open, scale-invariant set $\{s \neq 0\}$ of the null cone, so it descends to a continuous map on the quotient. For the lift, $\dsc[X(x)] = x/1 = x$. Conversely, given a non-ideal $[N]$, normalise $s = 1$; the incidence condition \claimref{transport.swap-rescale-normal-form} then forces $t = \tfrac12 Q(x)$, so the normalised representative is exactly $X(x)$ with $x = \dsc[N]$, whence $X(\dsc[N]) \in [N]$. Both directions are continuous, giving the homeomorphism.

(2) By Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}(2), $\iota[X(x)] = [X(\rho(x))]$, and $\dsc[X(\rho(x))] = \rho(x)$ by (1).

(3) Immediate from Theorem \claimref{transport.totality}(3) and the definition of the ideal points.

transport.door-one-way.formal: Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ be nondegenerate and let $B$ be either minimal completion of this paper: the Rule-1 ascent $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1) \cong \Mat_2(A)$, or (when $p - q \equiv 1 \bmod 4$) a Rule-2 ascent $\cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$. Then there is no unital algebra homomorphism $B \to A$ whatsoever. Every descent is therefore non-multiplicative; the conditional expectation of Proposition \claimref{transport.pinching-kernel} is the canonical linear surrogate, and its loss, the erasure of the ladder sector, is forced by the algebra, not chosen by the formalism.
transport.door-one-way.technical:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ be nondegenerate and let $B$ be either minimal completion: the Rule 1 ascent $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1) \cong \Mat_2(A)$, or, when $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, a Rule 2 ascent $\cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$. Then there is no unital algebra homomorphism $B \to A$ whatsoever.

Every descent from such a completion to its base is therefore non-multiplicative. The pinching conditional expectation is the canonical linear surrogate, and its loss, the erasure of the ladder sector, is forced by the algebra and not chosen by the formalism.
transport.door-one-way.lay: The series repairs an algebra by moving up to a larger one. Starting from a nondegenerate algebra, this result shows that there is no way back down that respects multiplication: no structure-preserving map from either larger algebra (the second kind exists only when the signature meets a congruence condition) to the original one exists. Any return journey must lose something, and the natural way back loses the part the climb added.
transport.door-one-way.typing_note: Added Rule 1 Morita triviality (the hypothesis and proof use the isomorphism of the Rule 1 ascent with Mat_2(A)) and the classification (semisimplicity of B and the split form of A); did not add the pinching-kernel context_ref, since the conditional expectation appears only as commentary after the no-homomorphism result. Levels pass: lay and one-liner now keep nondegeneracy and the congruence condition for the Rule 2 completion (the W503 trigger, "conditional expectation", was itself a false positive).

proofs.main: $B$ is semisimple (\claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}), so the kernel of a homomorphism $\theta : B \to A$ is a sum of Wedderburn blocks of $B$, and $\theta$ is injective on the complementary blocks; unitality ($\theta(1) = 1 \neq 0$) forces at least one block to survive. It suffices then that every block of $B$ has real dimension exceeding $\dim_\R A$. Rule 1, $A$ simple: $B \cong \Mat_2(A)$ (\claimref{transport.rule-1-morita-trivial}) is a single block of dimension $4 \dim A > \dim A$. Rule 1, $A = S \oplus S$ split: $\Mat_2(A) \cong \Mat_2(S) \oplus \Mat_2(S)$, blocks of dimension $4 \dim S = 2 \dim A > \dim A$. Rule 2 ($A$ split): $B \cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0)$ is simple (Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}) of dimension $2^{n+1} = 2\dim A > \dim A$. In every case no block embeds in $A$, contradiction.

transport.embedding-independent-minimali.formal:
Let $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $A = \Cl(p,q) \cong \Mat_k(\mathbb{F}) \oplus \Mat_k(\mathbb{F})$ with $\mathbb{F} \in \{\R, \HH\}$, $f = \dim_\R \mathbb{F}$, so $\dim_\R A = 2k^2 f = 2^n$. Let $B$ be any \emph{simple} finite-dimensional real algebra admitting a unital algebra embedding $A \hookrightarrow B$. Then
\[
\dim_\R B \;\geq\; 2^{\,n+1},
\]
and equality holds if and only if $B \cong \Mat_{2k}(\mathbb{F}) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$: the fused algebra of Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form} is the minimal simple environment of $A$ in the absolute sense, and it is the unique one of minimal dimension up to isomorphism.
transport.embedding-independent-minimali.technical:
Let $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, so that $A = \Cl(p,q) \cong \Mat_k(\mathbb{F}) \oplus \Mat_k(\mathbb{F})$ with $\mathbb{F} \in \{\R, \HH\}$ and $\dim_\R A = 2^n$. If $B$ is any simple finite-dimensional real algebra admitting a unital embedding $A \hookrightarrow B$, of whatever kind, then $\dim_\R B \geq 2^{n+1}$, with equality if and only if $B \cong \Mat_{2k}(\mathbb{F}) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$.

So the fused algebra of Rule 2 is the minimal simple environment of the split algebra in the absolute sense, not only among Clifford ascents, and it is the unique one of minimal dimension up to isomorphism.
transport.embedding-independent-minimali.lay: When a Clifford algebra splits into two halves, the series repairs it by adding one direction, which fuses the halves into a single indivisible algebra twice the size. This result shows that no cleverer choice does better: any indivisible algebra containing the split one is at least twice its size. The fused algebra is, up to relabelling, the only one that achieves this.
transport.embedding-independent-minimali.typing_note: Added the classification, which the hypothesis uses for the split form Mat_k(F) + Mat_k(F) and the proof for the irreducible modules; kept the corner and fusion premises used in the final identification.

proofs.main:
Write $B \cong \Mat_m(D)$, $D \in \{\R, \C, \HH\}$, $d = \dim_\R D$, with unique irreducible module $W = D^m$, $\dim_\R W = md$. $B$ acts faithfully on $W$, hence so does $A$; a faithful module of $A$, split as in the statement by \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}, contains both irreducibles $V_\pm$ (of $\dim_\R = kf$ each), since otherwise one of the central projectors $\varepsilon_\pm \neq 0$ would act as zero. So $W \cong V_+^{\,a} \oplus V_-^{\,b}$ as an $A$-module with $a, b \geq 1$ and
\[
md \;=\; (a + b)\,k f \;\geq\; 2kf .
\]
Moreover the right $D$-action on $W$ commutes with $A$, so $D$ embeds unitally in the commutant (strictly, the right action embeds $D^{\mathrm{op}}$; harmless, as $\R$, $\C$ and $\HH$ are each isomorphic to their opposites, and the dimension bounds below are opposite-invariant) $\mathrm{End}_A(W) \cong \Mat_a(\mathbb{F}) \oplus \Mat_b(\mathbb{F})$ (using $\mathrm{End}_{\Mat_k(\mathbb{F})}(\mathbb{F}^k) \cong \mathbb{F}$ as real algebras), hence, projecting to each summand, unitally in both $\Mat_a(\mathbb{F})$ and $\Mat_b(\mathbb{F})$.

Case $\mathbb{F} = \R$ ($f = 1$, $2k^2 = 2^n$). If $D = \R$: $m \geq 2k$ and $\dim B = m^2 \geq 4k^2 = 2^{n+1}$, with equality iff $m = 2k$, $B \cong \Mat_{2k}(\R)$. If $D = \C$: $\C \hookrightarrow \Mat_a(\R)$ forces $a \geq 2$, likewise $b \geq 2$, so $2m = (a+b)k \geq 4k$, $m \geq 2k$, and $\dim B = 2m^2 \geq 8k^2 = 2^{n+2}$. If $D = \HH$: $a, b \geq 4$, so $4m \geq 8k$, $\dim B = 4m^2 \geq 16k^2$. Case $\mathbb{F} = \HH$ ($f = 4$, $8k^2 = 2^n$). If $D = \HH$: $4m \geq 8k$ gives $m \geq 2k$ and $\dim B = 4m^2 \geq 16k^2 = 2^{n+1}$, equality iff $B \cong \Mat_{2k}(\HH)$. If $D = \C$: $\C \hookrightarrow \Mat_a(\HH)$ allows $a \geq 1$, but then $2m = 4(a+b)k \geq 8k$ gives $m \geq 4k$ and $\dim B = 2m^2 \geq 32k^2$. If $D = \R$: $m = 4(a+b)k \geq 8k$ and $\dim B = m^2 \geq 64k^2$. In every case the bound holds, and the equality case is exactly $\Mat_{2k}(\mathbb{F})$. Finally $\Mat_{2k}(\mathbb{F}) \cong \Mat_2(\Mat_k(\mathbb{F})) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$ by Lemma \claimref{transport.corner-even-subalgebra} and Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}.

transport.fusion-occurs-most-once.technical:
A transport history is a finite chain of algebras starting at a nondegenerate $\Cl(p,q)$, each step being Rule 1, the $(1,1)$ ascent, or, when the current algebra carries type C, Rule 2, ideal fusion. Rule 1 leaves the clock residue $d \bmod 8$ unchanged and Rule 2 moves it by $\pm 1$. Type C occurs exactly at $d \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, that is at residues $1$ and $5$, and Rule 2 sends these into $\{0, 2\}$ and $\{4, 6\}$, none of which is $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

Hence Rule 2 is applied at most once in any history, and after it, or from the start if $d \not\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, every later algebra has the same Wedderburn type. The physical case $\Cl(1,3)$ has $d \equiv 6$, is simple and never calls for Rule 2, and its Rule 1 ascents $\Cl(1{+}k, 3{+}k) \cong \Mat_{2^k}(\Cl(1,3))$ stay at residue $6$, of quaternionic type.
transport.fusion-occurs-most-once.lay: Each Clifford algebra sits at one of eight positions on a clock. One repair rule never moves the hand; the other moves it by one step, is only used at the two positions where the algebra is split, and always lands where no split occurs. So the second rule can be used at most once, after which nothing structural changes. The algebra of spacetime starts at a position that never needs the second rule.

The closing statement on $\Cl(1,3)$ reads its residue $6$, simple and quaternionic, off \claimref{transport.classification-real-clifford-algebras}.

transport.matrix-units-peirce-isomorphis.formal:
Let $\gamma = \pm 1$ and set
\[
E_{11} = \varepsilon_+, \qquad E_{22} = \varepsilon_-, \qquad E_{12} = \varepsilon_+ \nu, \qquad E_{21} = \gamma\, \varepsilon_- \nu .
\]
Then $E_{11} + E_{22} = 1$ and $E_{ij} E_{kl} = \delta_{jk} E_{il}$: a full $2 \times 2$ system of matrix units. Consequently
\[
B_\gamma \;\cong\; \Mat_2\bigl(E_{11} B_\gamma E_{11}\bigr), \qquad b \;\longmapsto\; \bigl(E_{1i}\, b\, E_{j1}\bigr)_{ij},
\]
an isomorphism of unital algebras with inverse $(c_{ij}) \mapsto \sum_{i,j} E_{i1} c_{ij} E_{1j}$.
transport.matrix-units-peirce-isomorphis.technical:
With $Q(
u) = \gamma = \pm 1$, set $E_{11} = \varepsilon_+$, $E_{22} = \varepsilon_-$, $E_{12} = \varepsilon_+ 
u$ and $E_{21} = \gamma\, \varepsilon_- 
u$. These satisfy $E_{11} + E_{22} = 1$ and $E_{ij} E_{kl} = \delta_{jk} E_{il}$, a full $2 	imes 2$ system of matrix units in $B_\gamma$.

Consequently $b \mapsto (E_{1i}\, b\, E_{j1})_{ij}$ is an isomorphism of unital algebras $B_\gamma \cong \Mat_2(E_{11} B_\gamma E_{11})$, with inverse $(c_{ij}) \mapsto \sum_{i,j} E_{i1} c_{ij} E_{1j}$.
transport.matrix-units-peirce-isomorphis.lay: Inside the enlarged algebra, the two projectors that used to split the original algebra, together with the new direction, behave exactly like the four basic entries of a two-by-two matrix. It follows that the enlarged algebra is the same thing as two-by-two matrices whose entries come from one corner of it.
transport.matrix-units-peirce-isomorphis.typing_note: Kept the single premise; the paper calls this the standard matrix-units criterion (Lam), reproved for self-containment, but no imported claim for it is in the store, so no standard-route derivation was added.

proofs.main:
The relations, using $\nu \varepsilon_\pm = \varepsilon_\mp \nu$ (Proposition \claimref{transport.ascent-renders-grade-involution-inner}), $\varepsilon_\pm^2 = \varepsilon_\pm$, $\varepsilon_+\varepsilon_- = 0$, $\nu^2 = \gamma$ and $\gamma^2 = 1$:
\begin{align*}
E_{12}E_{21} &= \varepsilon_+ \nu\, \gamma \varepsilon_- \nu = \gamma\, \varepsilon_+ (\nu \varepsilon_-) \nu = \gamma\, \varepsilon_+ \varepsilon_+ \nu^2 = \gamma^2 \varepsilon_+ = E_{11},\\
E_{21}E_{12} &= \gamma\, \varepsilon_- \nu\, \varepsilon_+ \nu = \gamma\, \varepsilon_-^2 \nu^2 = E_{22},
\end{align*}
and the remaining relations follow the same way:
\[
E_{12}^2 = \varepsilon_+ \nu \varepsilon_+ \nu = \varepsilon_+ \varepsilon_- \nu^2 = 0, \qquad E_{21}^2 = 0,
\]
\[
E_{11}E_{12} = E_{12}, \qquad
E_{12}E_{11} = \varepsilon_+ \nu \varepsilon_+ = \varepsilon_+\varepsilon_-\nu = 0 .
\] For the Peirce isomorphism, write $\phi(b)_{ij} = E_{1i} b E_{j1} \in E_{11} B_\gamma E_{11}$. Multiplicativity, using $E_{k1}E_{1k} = E_{kk}$ and $E_{11} + E_{22} = 1$:
\[
\sum_k \phi(b)_{ik}\,\phi(b')_{kj}
\;=\; \sum_k E_{1i}\, b\, E_{k1}E_{1k}\, b'\, E_{j1}
\;=\; E_{1i}\, b \Bigl(\textstyle\sum_k E_{kk}\Bigr) b'\, E_{j1}
\;=\; \phi(bb')_{ij} .
\]
Unitality: $\phi(1)_{ij} = E_{1i}E_{j1} = \delta_{ij} E_{11}$. The displayed inverse is checked directly:
\[
\sum_{i,j} E_{i1}\, (E_{1i}\, b\, E_{j1})\, E_{1j} \;=\; \Bigl(\textstyle\sum_i E_{ii}\Bigr)\, b\, \Bigl(\textstyle\sum_j E_{jj}\Bigr) \;=\; b ,
\]
and conversely on matrices. This is the standard matrix-units criterion \cite{LamFC2001}, reproved for self-containment.

transport.minimality.formal:
Let $(\mathbb{W}, f)$ be any null-lift completion of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$. Then $\mathbb{W}$ contains at least one direction of positive square and one of negative square; in particular $\dim \mathbb{W} \geq 2$, and enlargements of signature increment $(+k, 0)$ or $(0, +k)$ are excluded for every $k$. A single hyperbolic plane suffices, and any two-dimensional $\mathbb{W}$ admitted by the definition is a hyperbolic plane; hence the minimal completion is
\[
\Cl(p,q) \;\longrightarrow\; \Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1),
\]
with the adjoined space unique up to isometry, and the signature increment is $(+1,+1)$ in every signature.
transport.minimality.technical:
A null-lift completion of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ is a nondegenerate quadratic space $\mathbb{W}$ adjoined orthogonally, with a map $f : \mathbb{V} \to \mathbb{W}$, $f(0) \neq 0$, such that $X(x) = f(x) + x$ is null for every $x$. For any such completion, $\mathbb{W}$ contains a direction of positive square and one of negative square, so $\dim \mathbb{W} \geq 2$ and enlargements of increment $(+k, 0)$ or $(0, +k)$ are excluded for every $k$.

A single hyperbolic plane suffices, and any two-dimensional admissible $\mathbb{W}$ is a hyperbolic plane. Hence the minimal completion is $\Cl(p,q) \to \Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$, with the adjoined space unique up to isometry and increment $(+1,+1)$ in every signature.
transport.minimality.lay: To make the reciprocal work everywhere, the series represents each point as a light-like direction in a larger space. This result asks how much larger that space has to be. The added part must contain at least one direction of positive square and one of negative square, so adding only space-like or only time-like directions never works, while one such pair is enough and is essentially unique.
transport.minimality.typing_note: No claim premises (the proof uses classical facts about quadratic spaces from Lam and the definition of a null-lift completion); the paper presents the result as new, so there is no standard route.

proofs.main:
Nullity of $X(x)$ and orthogonality of $\mathbb{W}$ to $\mathbb{V}$ give
\[
Q_{\mathbb{W}}(f(x)) = -Q(x) \qquad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{V}.
\]
Setting $x = 0$: $Q_{\mathbb{W}}(f(0)) = 0$ with $f(0) \neq 0$, so $\mathbb{W}$ contains a nonzero null vector. A nondegenerate quadratic space containing a nonzero null vector is indefinite \cite{Lam2005} (a null vector has a hyperbolic partner, \claimref{std-algebra.witt-decomposition}), hence contains directions of both signs and has dimension at least $2$; increments $(+k,0)$ and $(0,+k)$, whose forms are definite, are excluded for every $k$. (When $\mathbb{V}$ has mixed signature the same conclusion follows a second way, with no appeal to the origin: $-Q$ attains both signs, hence so does $Q_{\mathbb{W}}$.)

Sufficiency of one hyperbolic plane is the construction of the section “The completion: the conformal model”--the section “Totality of the transported reciprocal”. For uniqueness of the minimal $\mathbb{W}$: a two-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space containing a nonzero null vector is indefinite, hence of signature $(1,1)$, and is the hyperbolic plane, unique up to isometry (the section “Null vectors, zero divisors, and hyperbolic planes”, \cite{Lam2005}; \claimref{std-algebra.sylvester-inertia}). Hence $\dim \mathbb{W} = 2$ with signature $(1,1)$ is minimal and unique, and the increment is $(+1,+1)$.

transport.no-fourth-rule.formal: The taxonomy of Definition \claimref{obj.transport.obstruction-types} is transport-complete with two nontrivial rules. Type N: ascend by one hyperbolic plane, with the repair delivered at the level of points (Theorems \claimref{transport.no-go-level-elements}, \claimref{transport.totality}, \claimref{transport.minimality}, \claimref{transport.representation-independent-minimality-completion}). Type C: ascend by one generator, with the fused algebra unique up to isomorphism (Theorems \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}, \claimref{transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-completions-classified}, \claimref{transport.embedding-independent-minimality-fusion}). Type P: no ascent; the identity is an equivariant repair (Proposition \claimref{transport.type-p-self-repairing}). By the exhaustiveness theorem (Theorem \claimref{transport.exhaustiveness-every-zero-divisor-annihilated-idempotent}), every zero divisor of a nondegenerate real Clifford algebra falls under these three rules.
transport.no-fourth-rule.technical:
The obstruction taxonomy is transport-complete with two nontrivial rules. Type N, a null vector with $Q(v) = 0$, is handled by ascending one hyperbolic plane, with the repair delivered at the level of points, as the no-go, totality and the two minimality theorems establish. Type C, a central idempotent, is handled by ascending one generator, with the fused algebra unique up to isomorphism and minimal. Type P, a non-central idempotent, needs no ascent: the identity is an equivariant repair.

By the exhaustiveness theorem every zero divisor of a nondegenerate real Clifford algebra falls under one of these three rules, so no fourth rule is needed.
transport.no-fourth-rule.lay: Division can fail in a nondegenerate real Clifford algebra in exactly three ways, and each has its own prescribed fix: add a pair of dimensions, add one dimension, or do nothing. Since every failure of division is one of the three, the list of fixes is complete.
transport.no-fourth-rule.typing_note: Kept all nine cited theorems: the corollary has no separate proof and is the conjunction of the results its statement names. Levels pass: the lay level now restricts the claim to nondegenerate real Clifford algebras, as the formal does.

transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-.formal:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$, $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and consider the Clifford algebras $\Cl(\mathbb{V}', Q')$ of arbitrary extensions $(\mathbb{V}', Q') \supseteq (\mathbb{V}, Q)$ of the quadratic space, $Q'$ possibly degenerate, each containing $A$ canonically and unitally. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\dim \mathbb{V}' = n$ (no ascent): $A$ itself is not simple (Theorem \claimref{transport.existence-classification-type-c}).
\item $\dim \mathbb{V}' = n + 1$, adjoined generator null ($\gamma = 0$): the fusion fails structurally. The subspace $J = A\nu$ is a nonzero proper two-sided ideal of $B_0$ with $J^2 = 0$, and $B_0 / J \cong A$: the degenerate ascent is an infinitesimal thickening of $A$, not a completion of it. (This square-zero ideal is the fibre-level germ of the degeneration sheaf of the series' sheaf-theoretic paper \cite{ButlerT4}.)
\item $\dim \mathbb{V}' = n + 1$, adjoined generator nondegenerate ($\gamma = \pm 1$ after rescaling): both ascents are simple and $\cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$ (Theorem \claimref{transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form}).
\item $\dim \mathbb{V}' \geq n + 2$: $\dim \Cl(\mathbb{V}') \geq 2^{n+2}$.
\end{enumerate}
Hence the minimal simple Clifford completions of $A$ are exactly the two one-generator ascents $\Cl(p{+}1,q)$ and $\Cl(p,q{+}1)$, of dimension $2^{n+1}$; they are inequivalent as quadratic data (the extensions $\langle +1 \rangle$ and $\langle -1 \rangle$ are non-isometric) but isomorphic as algebras; and so the minimal completion of a type-C obstruction is \emph{unique up to isomorphism}, with the residual geometric choice, the sign of the adjoined direction's square, not detected by the completed algebra.
transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-.technical:
Let $A = \Cl(p,q)$ with $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, and consider the Clifford algebras of arbitrary extensions $(\mathbb{V}', Q') \supseteq (\mathbb{V}, Q)$, $Q'$ possibly degenerate. With no ascent, $A$ is not simple. Adjoining one null generator ($\gamma = 0$) fails structurally: $J = A\nu$ is a nonzero proper two-sided ideal of $B_0$ with $J^2 = 0$ and $B_0/J \cong A$, an infinitesimal thickening rather than a completion. Adjoining one nondegenerate generator ($\gamma = \pm 1$ after rescaling) gives a simple algebra $\cong \Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$. Adjoining two or more directions gives dimension at least $2^{n+2}$.

Hence the minimal simple Clifford completions of $A$ are exactly $\Cl(p{+}1,q)$ and $\Cl(p,q{+}1)$, of dimension $2^{n+1}$. They differ as quadratic data, since $\langle +1 \rangle$ and $\langle -1 \rangle$ are not isometric, but are isomorphic as algebras, so the minimal completion of a type-C obstruction is unique up to isomorphism and does not detect the sign of the adjoined direction.
transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-.lay: When a Clifford algebra splits into two halves, one can try to repair it by adding directions. Adding nothing leaves it split; adding one direction of zero length only thickens the algebra without joining the halves; adding one direction of nonzero length joins them; adding more is larger than needed. The two possible single directions, of positive or negative square, give the same algebra, so the repair is unique and cannot tell which sign was used.
transport.one-generator-minimal-minimal-.typing_note: Kept all three premises, each invoked for a numbered clause.

transport.representation-independent-min.formal:
Let $(\mathbb{V}'', Q'')$ be nondegenerate of signature $(p'', q'')$ and suppose its null cone admits a normalised conformal chart of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$. Then
\[
p'' \geq p + 1 \quad \text{and} \quad q'' \geq q + 1 ;
\]
in particular $\dim \mathbb{V}'' \geq n + 2$, and in case of equality the signature is exactly $(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ and $\Cl(\mathbb{V}'') \cong \Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$. Consequently the minimality of the completion is a property of the ambient quadric alone: no Clifford algebra whose quadratic space is smaller than, or differently balanced than, $(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ can host the point-level resolution, \emph{however} $\Cl(p,q)$ is embedded in it as an algebra.
transport.representation-independent-min.technical:
Let $(\mathbb{V}'', Q'')$ be nondegenerate of signature $(p'', q'')$, and suppose its null cone carries a normalised conformal chart of $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$, a map $\Phi$ with $\Phi(x) \cdot \Phi(y) = -\frac12 Q(x - y)$. Then $p'' \geq p + 1$ and $q'' \geq q + 1$, so $\dim \mathbb{V}'' \geq n + 2$, and in the equality case the signature is exactly $(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ and $\Cl(\mathbb{V}'') \cong \Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1)$.

The minimality of the completion is thus a property of the ambient quadric alone: no Clifford algebra whose quadratic space is smaller than, or differently balanced than, $(p{+}1, q{+}1)$ can host the point-level resolution, however $\Cl(p,q)$ is embedded in it as an algebra.
transport.representation-independent-min.lay: One might hope to repair a geometry inside some smaller algebra by placing the original algebra in it in an unusual way. This result rules that out. What the repair needs is room for the points of the geometry together with their separations, and that requires at least one extra positive and one extra negative direction, whatever the embedding.
transport.representation-independent-min.typing_note: Kept the single premise, the conformal Gram matrix lemma, which the proof uses for the rank and signature count.

proofs.main: Let $s_i = \Phi(p_i)$ for the points of Lemma \claimref{transport.conformal-gram-matrix}. The chart condition gives $s_i \cdot s_j = M_{ij}$, so the pullback of $Q''|_{\mathrm{span}\{s_i\}}$ to $\R^{n+2}$ along $(c_i) \mapsto \sum c_i s_i$ is the quadratic form of $M$. Since $M$ is nondegenerate (Lemma \claimref{transport.conformal-gram-matrix}), the map is injective, the span $S$ has dimension $n+2$, and $Q''|_S$ is nondegenerate of signature $(p{+}1, q{+}1)$. A nondegenerate subspace splits off orthogonally, $\mathbb{V}'' = S \perp S^\perp$, whence $p'' = (p{+}1) + p(S^\perp) \geq p+1$ and likewise for $q''$. Equality of dimensions forces $S = \mathbb{V}''$ and the signature claim; the algebra statement is the functoriality of $\Cl$ on isometries.

transport.rule-1-morita-trivial.formal:
The elements
\[
E_{11} = ff^*, \qquad E_{22} = f^*f, \qquad E_{12} = f, \qquad E_{21} = f^*
\]
form a full $2 \times 2$ system of matrix units in $B$ ($E_{11} + E_{22} = 1$, $E_{ij}E_{kl} = \delta_{jk}E_{il}$); the corner is the base, $E_{11} B E_{11} = A\,ff^* \cong A$ via $a \mapsto a\,ff^*$; and therefore
\[
\Cl(p{+}1, q{+}1) \;\cong\; \Mat_2\bigl(\Cl(p,q)\bigr),
\]
under which the ascent embedding $A \hookrightarrow B$ becomes the twisted diagonal $a \mapsto \mathrm{diag}(a, \hat{a})$. In particular Rule 1 preserves the Morita class: the Wedderburn type, and with it the simplicity or splitness and the type-C diagnosis of the section “A taxonomy of obstructions”, are the same for $B$ as for $A$, and the clock residue $d = p - q \pmod 8$ is fixed. (The \emph{presence} of types N and P is not preserved and could not be: Proposition \claimref{transport.no-transport-terminates} below shows every completion carries fresh obstructions of its own.) The adjoined ladder pair is, in the matrix description, exactly the off-diagonal matrix units, and the descent projectors $f^*f,\, ff^*$ are the diagonal ones.
transport.rule-1-morita-trivial.technical:
Let Rule 1 adjoin a hyperbolic pair $f, f^*$ to $A = \Cl(p,q)$, giving $B = \Cl(p+1, q+1)$. Then $E_{11} = ff^*$, $E_{22} = f^*f$, $E_{12} = f$, $E_{21} = f^*$ form a full system of $2 \times 2$ matrix units in $B$, whose corner is the base, $E_{11} B E_{11} = A\,ff^* \cong A$. Therefore $\Cl(p+1, q+1) \cong \Mat_2(\Cl(p,q))$, under which the ascent embedding becomes the twisted diagonal $a \mapsto \mathrm{diag}(a, \hat a)$.

So Rule 1 preserves the Morita class: the Wedderburn type, simplicity or splitness, the type-C diagnosis and the clock residue $d = p - q \pmod 8$ are unchanged, although the presence of obstructions of types N and P is not preserved. In the matrix picture the adjoined ladder pair is the off-diagonal matrix units and the descent projectors $f^*f$, $ff^*$ are the diagonal ones.
transport.rule-1-morita-trivial.lay: The basic transport step adds one new pair of null directions to an algebra. The enlarged algebra turns out to be the algebra of two-by-two matrices with entries in the original one, with the new null pair playing the role of the off-diagonal entries. So the step leaves the essential type of the algebra unchanged, although whether certain other kinds of obstruction are present can change.
transport.rule-1-morita-trivial.typing_note: Kept the Peirce isomorphism; the no-termination proposition is cited only to contrast what is not preserved, so not added. The final step uses classical Morita equivalence of A and M_2(A), which the store holds only as a later-paper import, so no edge was added for it. Levels pass: conditions already kept.

proofs.main: The matrix-unit relations are the hyperbolic-pair identities $v^2 = w^2 = 0, \qquad vw + wv = 1, \qquad \text{hence} \quad vwv = (1 - wv)v = v$ read off directly: $E_{12}E_{21} = ff^* = E_{11}$, $E_{21}E_{12} = f^*f = E_{22}$, $E_{12}^2 = f^2 = 0 = E_{21}^2$, $E_{11}E_{12} = ff^*f = f = E_{12}$, $E_{12}E_{11} = f\,ff^* = 0$, and so on; $E_{11} + E_{22} = 1$ is the pair's anticommutator. For the corner: using the displayed decomposition of $B$ and $ff^* a = a\, ff^*$ (evenness), one computes $ff^* (a_0 + a_1 f + a_2 f^* + a_3 ff^*)\, ff^* = (a_0 + a_3) ff^*$, since $ff^* \cdot f \cdot ff^* = f f^* Q(f) f^* = f \cdot ff^* = f^2 f^* = 0$ and likewise the $f^*$ term vanishes, while the $1$ and $ff^*$ terms remain; so $E_{11}BE_{11} = A\,ff^*$. The map $a \mapsto a\,ff^*$ is an algebra isomorphism onto it: multiplicative since $(a\,ff^*)(b\,ff^*) = ab\,(ff^*)^2 = ab\,ff^*$, unital onto the corner unit $ff^*$, injective by the directness of the decomposition. The Peirce isomorphism of Lemma \claimref{transport.matrix-units-peirce-isomorphism}, whose proof uses only the matrix-unit relations, then gives $B \cong \Mat_2(A)$. The embedding: for $a \in A$, $\varphi(a)_{11} = E_{11} a E_{11} = a\,ff^*$ and $\varphi(a)_{22} = E_{12}\, a\, E_{21} = f a f^* = \hat{a}\, ff^*$, while the off-diagonal entries vanish ($E_{11} a E_{21} = a\, ff^*f^* = 0$, $E_{12} a E_{11} = \hat a\,f ff^* = 0$); under the corner identification this is $\mathrm{diag}(a, \hat{a})$, which is multiplicative since the grade involution is an automorphism (\claimref{std-algebra.involution-properties}). Morita-class preservation, and with it the invariance of the type-C diagnosis, is the statement $\Mat_2(A) \sim_{\text{Morita}} A$ (\claimref{std-algebra.morita-amplification}) together with the fact that the Wedderburn data of $\Mat_2(\Mat_m(D))$ (or of the split case, blockwise) is that of $A$ with $m$ doubled.

transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form.formal:
Let $p - q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $\gamma = \pm 1$. Then
\[
B_\gamma \;=\; \Cl(p{+}1,q) \ \text{or}\ \Cl(p,q{+}1) \;\cong\; \Mat_2\bigl(\Cl^0(p,q)\bigr),
\]
by the matrix units of Lemma \claimref{transport.matrix-units-peirce-isomorphism} and the corner identification of Lemma \claimref{transport.corner-even-subalgebra}. Consequently:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $B_\gamma$ is simple, and its centre is $\R$: the fusion does not reintroduce a central splitting, and $B_\gamma$ carries no type-C obstruction.
\item The images of $\varepsilon_\pm$ in $B_\gamma$ are a conjugate pair of non-central idempotents, the diagonal matrix units of the fused algebra, exchanged by the inner automorphism $\mathrm{Ad}_\nu$, which restricts on $A$ to the grade involution (Proposition \claimref{transport.ascent-renders-grade-involution-inner}).
\item The two ascents are isomorphic as algebras: $\Cl(p{+}1,q) \cong \Cl(p,q{+}1)$, both canonically $\Mat_2(\Cl^0(p,q))$, with an isomorphism through the matrix units that fixes the corner.
\end{enumerate}

transport.rule-2-ideal-fusion-sharp-form.lay: Some Clifford algebras split into two independent halves. Adding one new direction, of either sign, fuses the halves into a single algebra of two-by-two matrices whose entries come from the algebra's even part. The fused algebra has no split of its own, and the two choices of sign give the same algebra.

transport.totality.technical:
Let $(\mathbb{V}, Q)$ be nondegenerate, with completion $\Cl(p{+}1,q{+}1)$ and quadric $\mathcal{Q}$ of null rays, and define $\iota[N] = [\, e_+ N e_+ \,]$. Then $\iota$ is well defined, total, continuous and an involution on $\mathcal{Q}$, and for $Q(x) 
eq 0$ it is the geometric reciprocal: $\iota[X(x)] = [X(x/Q(x))]$.

For $Q(x_0) = 0$, a null vector or the origin, $\iota[X(x_0)] = [\, x_0 +  rac12 
Inf \,]$, an ideal point ($[
Inf]$ when $x_0 = 0$), and this value is the limit of $\iota[X(x)]$ along every path of invertible $x 	o x_0$. Consequently $\iota$ is the unique continuous map of $\mathcal{Q}$ that agrees with the lifted reciprocal on the lifted invertible locus.
transport.totality.lay: In a Clifford algebra with vectors of zero length, the reciprocal of a vector is undefined on exactly those vectors. After moving to the enlarged space of points, a single reflection-like operation gives a reciprocal everywhere: it agrees with the usual one on ordinary vectors and sends zero-length vectors to points at infinity. Those values are the limits one would expect, and no other continuous rule matches the usual reciprocal.
